Subscribe another address With event costs up and funding down, journalism organizations cancel conferences and cut staff ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.” Byeeeee. (Adobe Stock) By Laura Hazard Owen Nov. 12, 2026, 1:09 p.m. RELATED ARTICLE We know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus? Joshua Benton March 25, 2020 When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid . For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously. At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them. Journalism organizations’ revenue, 2019–2025 Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026. The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers . “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.” LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added. LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program . But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.” “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said. OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode” 1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.” The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON , is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.” The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote. Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News , its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [ ↩ ] Get Nieman Lab’s Daily Digest The most important stories about journalism and the future of news, delivered to your inbox every afternoon. Subscribe Laura Hazard Owen is the editor of Nieman Lab. You can reach her via email , Bluesky , or Signal (laurahazardowen.38). November 12, 2026 See more on   Business & Revenue Tags Chris Krewson Institute for Nonprofit News IRE LION Publishers Niketa Patel ONA OpenNews SRCCON The latest from Nieman Lab Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted. A new study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk. Joshua Benton Some local news outlets are losing physical newsrooms Hanaa' Tameez AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news. results.title: Ohio Midterms Prove ‘Pink Slime’ News Is Bipartisan
results.pageTitle: Ohio Midterms Prove ‘Pink Slime’ News Is Bipartisan - Columbia Journalism Review
results.pageDescription: NorthStar Civic Media promises “independent local reporting.” Its founder worked on Democratic campaigns, and Democratic funders spent more than a million dollars on Meta ads promoting one of its sites.
results.evidenceText: Ohio Midterms Prove ‘Pink Slime’ News Is Bipartisan - Columbia Journalism Review b Wikimedia Commons / Adobe Stock / Illustration by CJR b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . Last month, when the Ohio gubernatorial campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy, a Republican, released an ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic challenger, Amy Acton, now the governor-elect, two websites styled as local news outlets covered the story from opposite political perspectives. The Buckeye Bulletin paid to boost the video on Facebook, while TiffinOhio.net ran stories on the Republican backlash, including a call from Governor Mike DeWine to pull the ad.  The Los Angeles Times later connected Buckeye Bulletin to the Lincoln Media Foundation, a nonprofit affiliated with the Lincoln Club, which the Times described as “the oldest and largest conservative donor organization in California.” TiffinOhio is one of six sites run by NorthStar Civic Media, whose registered address is a Chicago apartment. An analysis from the Tow Center for Digital Journalism found that, between early August and Election Day, Democratic groups spent more than a million dollars on Facebook ads promoting TiffinOhio stories. TiffinOhio and Buckeye Bulletin are two of more than sixty websites that look like Ohio local news outlets but are run by partisan networks, according to our review of business records, domain registrations, and Meta ad data. Many of the sites are examples of what researchers call pink slime: partisan content disguised as local journalism. Ahead of the midterms, these sites were used to reach voters in Ohio’s races for governor and the United States Senate, including through paid advertisements on social media. But their reach extends further, according to NewsGuard, which found that leading AI chatbots cited pink-slime sites nearly half the time when asked about midterm candidates and issues. TiffinOhio consists mostly of stories republished from established newsrooms. Its original articles are largely critical of Republicans—including Ramaswamy , Jon Husted , a Republican senator, Derek Merrin , a former state representative, and Gary Click , a current state representative—and credited either to the publisher, Dylan Poe, or to four staff reporters whose identities Tow Center researchers could not independently verify. Poe worked for the 2018 Senate campaign of Sherrod Brown, the 2012 presidential campaign of Barack Obama, and the Ohio Democratic Party, according to a 2020 Marion Star report . In response to emailed questions, Poe said that while his “background in political work is a matter of public record,” NorthStar, which he founded under a different name in 2024, “proudly operates a network of freely accessible news websites. We stand behind our reporting and believe our work should be evaluated on its factual accuracy, sourcing, and public-interest value.”  The NorthStar network shares several traits of pink slime: generic local names, nearly identical content across sites, a pre-election expansion, staff reporters who could not be identified, undisclosed funding, and heavy promotion by political groups. Poe denied that TiffinOhio is pink slime, saying the site has “proudly served Tiffin, Seneca County, and other Northwest Ohio communities for over ten years.” He pointed instead to sites like Buckeye Bulletin and Ohio Pulse as “actual ‘pink slime’ websites.” Among the Ohio partisan sites Tow Center researchers reviewed, most of those that ran ads paid to promote themselves. TiffinOhio was the exception. The site spent about thirteen hundred dollars on Facebook ads between August 4 and November 2. During the same period, outside groups spent far more promoting its stories.  Nearly all of that outside money came from Democratic-aligned groups and campaigns, including Acton’s campaign for governor, the American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees’ (AFSCME) Ohio political fund, the House Majority PAC, and WinSenate, a super-PAC funded almost entirely by the Democratic Senate Majority PAC, according to FactCheck.org. WinSenate alone spent between eight hundred and ninety-four thousand and 1.06 million dollars, much of it on ads promoting a TiffinOhio story that connected Husted to House Bill 6, a 2019 law that added fees to Ohioans’ electric bills to bail out nuclear and coal plants. Federal prosecutors later found that the nuclear plants’ operator had secured passage of the bill with more than sixty million dollars in bribes . (Husted has not been charged in connection with the scheme, and has denied involvement.)  TiffinOhio states on its website that it accepts no money from political parties, committees, candidates, or campaigns. Instead, it says, it is funded by readers, “limited earned revenue” and “mission-aligned partners,” which it describes as “organizations that share our commitment to democracy and local journalism.” It does not state who those partners are, or how much they contribute, and Poe declined to identify them.   A review of campaign finance and union records found no direct payments to Poe, NorthStar Civic Media, Tiffin Publishing, or any of its websites. In his email to the Tow Center, Poe said “third parties are free to share or promote” NorthStar’s work, and that “advertising expenditures by outside organizations should not be conflated with funding received by NorthStar Civic Media.” Beyond paid ads, NorthStar’s stories have been cited in Wikipedia entries. Since August, one editor has added six NorthStar articles, most of them critical of Ramaswamy, to entries on Ramaswamy and Ohio’s 2026 gubernatorial and House races. Two of those references, from the Cleveland Monitor , another NorthStar publication, were added four days before Election Day. (Poe said no one “involved with” NorthStar added the citations.) As of November 10, of the seventy-five authors listed on TiffinOhio —the only NorthStar site with an author page —five, including Poe, were identified as staffers. Around a quarter of the site’s articles are attributed to these authors; unlike Poe, the other four staff reporters had no photos on the author page. The Tow Center could not find LinkedIn profiles, bylines at other publications, or public records to verify their journalism careers. When asked about the site’s reporters, Poe said they are “real people,” and that “the absence of publicly available photographs or professional profiles should not be interpreted as evidence that these individuals do not exist.” He did not answer a question from Tow Center researchers about whether any of their work is produced with AI tools. The other seventy names on the author page referred to reporters or commentators for other outlets such as Signal Ohio and the nonprofit Ohio Capital Journal (OCJ) and its parent, States Newsroom , whose work is republished on TiffinOhio and its sister sites. In response to questions from Tow Center researchers, Lara Weber, the communications director for States Newsroom, wrote in an email that “None of us at OCJ or States Newsroom were aware of the ‘writers and contributors’ list they have posted, and no one from OCJ or States Newsroom agreed to it.” After the Tow Center’s inquiry, Weber said States Newsroom asked Poe to remove its journalists from the author lists on all of NorthStar’s sites, “as we have no partnership or other arrangement that would allow that.” She said Poe confirmed that NorthStar would do so. TiffinOhio initially removed just the names of authors from States Newsroom and OCJ from the author page; by November 11, the page was taken down. (Poe said TiffinOhio ’s content management system had “automatically added the authors to our author archive,” and that NorthStar had “never claimed a partnership or arrangement with States Newsroom beyond their standard republishing permissions.” Signal Ohio did not respond to Tow’s request for comment.) David DeWitt, the OCJ’s editor in chief, was among those listed on TiffinOhio ’s author page. He said he had seen TiffinOhio ’s articles but “was not aware of their author list” before the Tow Center contacted him, and that he has had no arrangement with the site beyond the OCJ’s standard republishing guidelines , which allow other outlets to republish its stories with credit. DeWitt’s only contact with NorthStar, he said, was an email he sent notifying the site that the OCJ had updated an article that TiffinOhio had republished.  Six of the authors who were listed on the TiffinOhio author page earlier this month are reporters for the Ohio Independent and its parent network, the American Independent Foundation, a Democratic Party–aligned 501(c)(4), some of whose publications have been classified as pink slime. Unlike 501(c)(3) nonprofits, its classification allows for political advocacy. TiffinOhio has republished twenty-one articles from the Ohio Independent and three from the American Independent .  Along with TiffinOhio and the Cleveland Monitor , NorthStar Civic Media owns Seneca Live and the Toledo Ledger , Columbus Wire , and Cincy Current . TiffinOhio has about sixty-seven thousand Facebook followers; Seneca Live has about forty-eight hundred. The other four sites don’t appear to have Facebook pages. Almost all the same headlines and articles run across the sites, but Seneca Live is the only site with a disclaimer: “Fifty headlines syndicated from TiffinOhio.net. Full stories are published at TiffinOhio.net.” The Fostoria Free Press , an Ohio outlet whose articles carry the byline “FFP Ai Bot,” appears to be the only site that has published substantial information about NorthStar’s connection to TiffinOhio . On its website, NorthStar says its mission is “empowering local journalism in the Great Lakes region” by offering “timely news” alongside “progressive analysis.” Editions in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin are “coming soon,” according to NorthStar, and Indiana, Illinois, and Minnesota are “on the roadmap.” According to the Tow Center’s review, Poe started TiffinOhio.net in 2016 and formed Tiffin Publishing LLC in 2020. In October of 2023, he announced that the site was closing because the pandemic had “led to decreased advertising revenue.” He dissolved the company three months later, but the site was soon publishing again. In October of 2024, Poe formed a new company in Chicago, DJP Holdings LLC; in March of 2025, it was renamed NorthStar Civic Media. Poe is listed as its only manager, and signed every filing reviewed for this report. On August 21, 2026, roughly ten weeks before the midterms, domains for the Cleveland, Columbus, and Toledo sites were registered. The Cincinnati domain was registered two days later. The expansion occurred shortly before Northwest Ohio’s largest newspaper, The Blade , in Toledo, announced its possible closure. (In September, the paper’s owner, Block Communications, said The Blade would shut down on December 31 unless a buyer was found, citing years of financial losses.)  The 2020 Marion Star report that identified Poe’s previous political work cites his LinkedIn profile, which is no longer online. It also includes a quote from Melissa Ackison, who was then a Republican state senate candidate: “We also have the help of Dylan Poe, who writes the Tiffin paper,” she says, according to an edited audio recording released by her primary opponent. “He’s helped me. He’s written op-eds for me.” The recording continues: “He has said, ‘We know a Republican’s going to hold this district. At least with you, we’ll get a seat at the table.’” Tiffin Publishing said at the time that it did not coordinate with any campaign. Ackison said her opponent’s allegation was “full of lies,” but did not directly address the claims about Poe. Since the Tow Center’s first published research into pink-slime networks in 2019, partisan groups have increasingly used local news-like sites as campaign vehicles. Other partisan networks targeting Ohio have been documented before by the Tow Center and other researchers. Metric Media , a conservative network tied to Brian Timpone, a former broadcast news reporter with a history of establishing publishing companies that use “ proprietary technology to transform public records into news,” publishes at least fifty-two Ohio-branded sites. Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super-PAC that NewsGuard found targeting Michigan voters last month, also funds Ohio Pulse , which spent more than five hundred thousand dollars on Meta ads between early August and Election Day.  Sthavir Murthy contributed research. Has America ever needed a media defender more than now? Help us by joining CJR today . About the Tow Center The Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia's Graduate School of Journalism, a partner of CJR, is a research center exploring the ways in which technology is changing journalism, its practice and its consumption — as we seek new ways to judge the reliability, standards, and credibility of information online. Submit Sign In | Membership News Training Ethics Fact-Checking Media Literacy AI Events Future of Public Media Newmark Ethics Center IFCN MediaWise PolitiFact Donate About Us Press Freedom Watch The Poynter 50 Podcasts Artificial Intelligence Business & Work Reporting & Editing Fact-Checking Ethics & Trust Local News Journalism, Media & Communication Training Poynter Membership Categories Consulting & Coaching For ACES Members For Local News Funders All Categories Broadcast & Visual Journalism Business & Work Ethics Fact-Checking & Media Literacy Leadership Reporting & Editing Writing Poynter ACES Introductory Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Intermediate Certificate in Editing Poynter ACES Advanced Certificate in Editing Workshops and Coaching Tools for Funders Ethics Ethics Training Ethics Articles AI Ethics Public Editor Project Get Ethics Advice Fact-Checking Articles IFCN IFCN Grants International Fact-Checking Day Teen Creator Network PolitiFact MediaWise Media Literacy Resources AI Literacy Ambassadors Teen Creator Network Research & News International en Español MediaWise Training All Events The 2026 Poynter Journalism Prizes Fact-Checking Voting stickers are displayed on Election Day in Missoula, Mont., Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Tommy Martino) By: Loreben Tuquero November 11, 2026 For two election cycles, misinformation and election experts have wondered: Will content generated with artificial intelligence dominate races and mislead voters? Campaigns and their supporters still use conventional ads to try to influence voters. But there were more AI-generated ads in the 2026 midterms compared with the 2024 election. And while this wasn’t “the ‘AI election’,” AI ads are the new normal, said Christina Walker, a University of Georgia international affairs assistant professor who studies how AI shapes political information. About 300 political ads were generated or enhanced by AI this election cycle, according to analysis by the Wesleyan Media Project, which tracks and analyzes political advertising. (AdImpact screenshots of AI-generated ads in the 2026 midterm elections.) And the people and groups behind those ads spent about $187 million promoting them online and on TV, the Wesleyan Media Project said — more than 3,000 times the approximate $50,000 spent during the 2024 election cycle. But that’s still a fraction of the overall political ad spending, which ad tracking service AdImpact projected at about $11.6 billion in 2025 and 2026. The Wesleyan Media Project said that about 90% of the ads it tracked came from Republican candidates or groups supporting them. Why campaigns did not go all out with AI ads in 2026 There’s an AI learning curve for campaigns and it’s time-consuming for them to become comfortable enough with new technologies to ensure voters are OK with it too, said Travis Ridout, Wesleyan Media Project’s co-director, so there’s “reputational risk” to consider. “You don’t want a voter backlash,” Ridout said. Polls show that voters don’t necessarily want political content produced with AI. A 2025 Pew Research Center study found that 71% of Americans said they would like a candidate less if they knew the candidate used AI to help write a speech they had otherwise enjoyed. “What people are okay with in terms of what AI is used for and how much it is used are still being worked out,” Walker said. Many of the ads were essentially a “new medium for creating political cartoons,” said Tim Harper, who works at the Center for Democracy & Technology leading policy and advocacy work related to election disinformation. Some AI ads fabricated information, others were more subtle Some campaign ads included deepfakes, fabricated videos that appear to show people saying or doing something that they didn’t. Other ads used AI to enhance or supplement real incidents, such as adding more people to a video of a crowd . Thirty-one states have laws regulating deepfakes in political messaging, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. Those rules are being actively tested, Harper said. Texas voters saw many ads with AI-generated visuals, including against state Rep. James Talarico , the Democratic candidate who won the state’s U.S. Senate race. Campaigns also crafted and distributed their talking points in ways that made it more likely for AI chatbots to surface that information to voters who ask questions about candidates and election issues. It’s difficult to gauge how much influence AI ads had on voters, who were inundated with many other messages on different platforms. “AI content isn’t necessarily persuading audiences,” said Cayce Myers, a Virginia Tech public relations professor, but it’s confirming already held opinions. AI still influenced voters, not because of the ways it helped produce political messaging, but based on concerns that the technology would lead to more data centers in their communities, depleting local resources, spiking energy bills and affecting their quality of life. results.evidenceText: WinSenate - FactCheck.org Skip to main content FactCheck .org ® A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center Political leanings: Democratic 2024 total spending: $313.1 million WinSenate is a super PAC that works to elect Democrats to the U.S. Senate. It was created during the 2024 election cycle and is affiliated with the Senate Majority PAC , or SMP, another liberal super PAC with the goal of helping Democrats win Senate races. Super PACs are allowed to raise and spend unlimited amounts of money on elections, as long as their contributions are not made to candidate committees and independent expenditures are not coordinated with candidate campaigns. Each super PAC must regularly report its expenditures and donations to the Federal Election Commission. During the 2024 elections, WinSenate received and spent about $313.1 million, with almost every dollar being contributed by the Senate Majority PAC. WinSenate spent nearly $311.3 million on independent expenditures , which are ads and other communications advocating for or against the election of a candidate. More than $287 million of that amount was spent against Republican Senate candidates, and about $24.2 million was spent supporting Democratic candidates, according to OpenSecrets, which tracks political spending. For the 2026 midterms, WinSenate reported receiving about $21.1 million – all from SMP – as of Aug. 31, according to its latest monthly filing with the FEC. It also reported spending almost $12.5 million on independent expenditures up to that point. But its receipts and spending in September appear to have surged, as this month WinSenate announced multiple multimillion dollar ad campaigns against Republican Senate candidates in Maine , Ohio , Iowa , North Carolina and New Hampshire . In fact, as of Sept. 24, according to data from the ad-tracking service AdImpact, WinSenate has spent or reserved more than $217 million on midterm ads, a huge increase from its prior spending this election cycle. Its next monthly financial report covering the month of September is due to the FEC on Oct. 20. Editor’s note: FactCheck.org does not accept advertising. We rely on grants and individual donations from people like you. Please consider a donation. Credit card donations may be made through our “Donate” page . If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102. Ask FactCheck Q: Are voting machines changing Democratic votes to Republican votes? Several posts on Facebook are making that claim. A: There is no evidence that touchscreen voting machines are deliberately switching voter selections. Rather, elections experts and state election officials have said that reported issues of machines initially not recording votes correctly are a result of familiar machine calibration issues or voter error. Also, nearly the entire country votes in a manner where voters review a paper ballot before having their votes officially cast. A new attack ad in the Ohio governor's race features the mother of the Democratic candidate, Amy Acton — estranged from her daughter over allegations of molestation by a stepfather — calling the candidate a liar. Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, confirmed to reporters Tuesday evening that the ad, which had not yet appeared on television, came from his campaign. Many Republicans hailed it as a bombshell after it began circulating on social media Monday night, while Democrats, and some Republicans, called it a new low by Mr. Ramaswamy in a campaign that was already one of the nation’s ugliest . Dr. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, condemned it as “despicable.” But Axios reported Tuesday night that the Ramaswamy campaign was investing $4 million to air the advertisement statewide. results.evidenceText: Rex Ryan arrested after allegedly hitting pedestrians with truck Skip to content Credit: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports By Matt Yoder on 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. ESPN NFL analyst Rex Ryan is facing four charges after being arrested following an incident in Nashville. According to The Tennesseean , Ryan was driving his pickup truck downtown when he allegedly ran over the feet of two pedestrians who were attempting to cross Broadway while the former coach was making a right turn. Of course, anyone in the know will find that to be incredibly ironic given Ryan’s well-documented love of that particular body part. Rex Ryan then drove away from the scene and was chased down by the pedestrians. According to the reports, Ryan then left his vehicle at a stop light to engage in an argument with them before driving away once again. Afterwards, the people who were hit took a photograph of the truck and its license plate and called police. It was later then traced back to Ryan, and he turned himself in to the authorities on Wednesday morning. Naturally, TMZ has already published a photo of his mug shot. The 63-year-old is now facing multiple charges stemming from the incident, including leaving the scene of an accident, failing to give information or render aid, and failing to obey a traffic signal. His bond was set at $6,000. When reached by Awful Announcing for comment about the situation, ESPN issued a statement that said, “We are aware and are in touch with Rex.” Ryan was head coach of the New York Jets and Buffalo Bills during his time in the NFL after winning a Super Bowl as defensive coordinator of the Baltimore Ravens. He has been an ESPN analyst since 2017 as one of the network’s top analysts, appearing on a number of shows including Sunday NFL Countdown and Get Up. Rex Ryan is a self-proclaimed “ toe expert ,” so if anyone should have checked on someone’s feet after being run over by a truck, then it should have been him. results.evidenceText: O fundo de florestas na COP31 e o trabalho sem direitos nas pedreiras Brasis Subscrever Entrar Translate O fundo de florestas na COP31 e o trabalho sem direitos nas pedreiras Uma curadoria do melhor do jornalismo digital, produzido pelas associadas à Ajor. Novos ângulos para assuntos do dia Brasis nov 12, 2026 6 Partilhar 🔸 “A verdade brutal é que a crise climática está nos superando”, disse o secretário-geral da ONU, António Guterres , durante a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia. Em sua última participação numa conferência do clima antes de deixar o cargo, no fim do ano, ele cobrou medidas urgentes para reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa, abandonar os combustíveis fósseis e ampliar o financiamento climático. O Eco destaca ainda que Guterres reconheceu que a ultrapassagem do limite de aquecimento global de 1,5°C, estabelecido pelo Acordo de Paris, tornou-se praticamente inevitável. Ele defendeu a criação de um Pacto Global de Justiça Climática, baseado em quatro pilares: acelerar a transição energética, proteger as populações vulneráveis, ampliar o financiamento climático e fortalecer a cooperação internacional. “Os poluidores devem pagar”, afirmou, ao defender a tributação dos lucros extraordinários das pretolíferas para financiar ações climáticas nos países mais vulneráveis. 🔸 O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) criticou o enfraquecimento da agenda climática internacional na abertura da COP31, informa a Agência Eixos . “As mudanças climáticas desapareceram dos discursos e documentos da liderança global. Nos fóruns de reuniões do G7 e do G20, que reúnem os maiores emissores de gases de efeito estufa do mundo, essa preocupação se transformou em silêncio”, afirmou. Segundo Lula, guerras, disputas comerciais e interesses econômicos têm dificultado a cooperação internacional. “Começamos a falar mais sobre armas e tarifas do que sobre a sobrevivência das gerações futuras.” O financiamento climático foi um ponto de divergência entre os líderes. A União Europeia defendeu que grandes economias, como a China, ampliem suas contribuições, enquanto o governo chinês reiterou que os países desenvolvidos devem assumir a maior responsabilidade pelo financiamento e pela redução das emissões. Obrigada por ler a Brasis. Gostou do conteúdo? Assine e compartilhe. Subscrever 🔸 Na conferência, uma coalizão de nove fundações e financiadores filantrópicos anunciou um aporte de US$ 88 milhões ao Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF), mecanismo de financiamento lançado pelo Brasil na COP30. Segundo o Reset , é o maior compromisso filantrópico recebido pelo fundo até agora. Com o anúncio, faltam US$ 2,1 bilhões para alcançar a meta de captação de US$ 10 bilhões até o fim de 2026. Entre os financiadores estão a Conservation International, a The Nature Conservancy e a Minderoo Foundation, do bilionário australiano Andrew Forrest, que ampliou sua contribuição para US$ 15 milhões. Durante o evento, Indonésia e Holanda reafirmaram compromissos de US$ 1 bilhão e US$ 500 milhões, respectivamente. “Esse anúncio mostra que o modelo está começando a funcionar”, disse o ministro das Relações Exteriores, Mauro Vieira. 🔸 Na volta da COP31, Lula deve anunciar quem vai substituir Andrei Rodrigues na direção-geral da Polícia Federal. Antes, porém, ele pretende definir primeiro quem comandará o futuro Ministério da Segurança Pública, conta a CartaCapital . A crise interna na PF, agravada por divergências entre delegados e pelos desdobramentos das investigações do Banco Master, pode acelerar a mudança. Nesta semana, Andrei deixou a Associação Nacional dos Delegados de Polícia Federal, da qual fazia parte havia mais de 20 anos. Entre os cotados para a direção da PF estão William Murad, atual diretor-executivo da corporação; Marcelo Werner, secretário de Segurança Pública da Bahia, apoiado pelo ministro da Justiça; e Helena de Rezende, diretora de Gestão de Pessoas da PF. A escolha está vinculada à criação do Ministério da Segurança Pública, prometido por Lula. Entre os possíveis ministros estão o promotor Lincoln Gakiya, conhecido pelo combate ao PCC, e o secretário nacional de Segurança Pública, Chico Lucas. 📮 Outras histórias Em Pedreiras (MA), o curso de Inclusão Digital para idosos ensinou os participantes a fazer pagamentos por Pix, identificar golpes virtuais, comprar passagens e usar mapas para a mobilidade. A formação faz parte da Universidade Aberta Intergeracional, programa de extensão da Universidade Estadual do Maranhão criado em 2016 para promover acesso a atividades socioeducativas e à troca de experiências. O Pedreirense acompanhou o encontro de conclusão do curso e mostra como os alunos viram as mudanças na maneira de lidar com as próprias dificuldades e de conquistar independência. 📌 Investigação Em Dona Inês, no Brejo paraibano, centenas de trabalhadores quebram granito à marreta no Lajedo da Serra. Sem carteira assinada e expostos ao sol, à poeira e a acidentes, eles sustentam a economia da cidade há mais de 60 anos. A Marco Zero revela como o trabalho se organiza numa hierarquia informal que passa de pai para filho. Josenildo Martins, o Bajau, aos 41 anos, já leva quase três décadas quebrando pedra. Começou aos 12, “fazendo brita”, quebrando, atividade também exercida pelo seu pai, Cícero Martins, hoje com 61 anos. As marcas no corpo também atravessam gerações. “Meu pai tem um medo danado de ficar cego”, diz Bajau sobre Cícero. Ele próprio já se cortou algumas vezes e carrega na perna uma cicatriz de um acidente que terminou com três pontos. Em um estudo realizado com 202 trabalhadores, 39,1% tinham queilite actínica, exposição crônica à radiação solar nos lábios que pode evoluir para câncer. Segundo uma fiscalização do Ministério Público do Trabalho na Paraíba, foram constatadas “várias irregularidades” relacionadas à saúde e à segurança dos trabalhadores e ao trabalho informal. 🍂 Meio ambiente A sensibilidade da Amazônia ao fogo necessita de ações transversais para impedir o alastramento dos incêndios florestais, como o Manejo Integrado do Fogo, que propõe unir prevenção, conhecimento do território, tecnologia e resposta para reduzir os riscos e os impactos. A Tipiti, newsletter da Abaré , explica como começam os incêndios – e sua relação com a falta de gestão adequada de resíduos sólidos – e como manejar o fogo depende do fortalecimento do senso de comunidade e da vigilância local. “Quando se discute apenas o incêndio florestal, gasta-se mais recursos, mais custos e perdem-se vidas. Se não discutirmos o fogo antes do incêndio acontecer, ficaremos eternamente apagando incêndios”, afirma Kurtis Bastos, chefe da Secretaria Permanente de Manejo Integrado do Fogo (SEPIF/Prevfogo) no Amazonas. Esta reportagem foi elaborada como parte do Programa de Líderes em Jornalismo de Soluções promovido pela Solutions Journalism Network (SJN) em parceria com a Associação de Jornalismo Digital (Ajor). 📙 Cultura “Trazer a ciência e a linguagem científica para dentro de um poema é só uma forma de brincar com as inúmeras possibilidades que a língua e o desejo de inventar e também comunicar nos permitem.” A poeta mineira Thaís Campolina constrói, por meio de corpos de outras espécies, de um peixe abissal a uma lagartixa, uma linguagem para falar da experiência humana. Em entrevista ao Le Monde Diplomatique Brasil , a autora fala sobre seu novo livro “Enxame”, que trata a memória como um registro inscrito nos corpos, humanos e não humanos. A obra é dividida em seções batizadas com nomes que permeiam agrupamentos animais: a colmeia, a onça, o bando, as rotas migratórias e o zumbido. “A estrutura nasceu do desejo de pensar o livro como um organismo vivo e móvel.” 🎧 Podcast Um dos principais responsáveis pela fama da culinária mineira, o chef Ivo Faria atravessou o preconceito contra a própria profissão e o racismo no mercado de trabalho. No início da carreira, a cor da pele e a aparência influenciavam as oportunidades de emprego nos restaurantes. “A profissão de cozinheiro não era uma profissão digna, era subemprego, era de cor e feio. Ia pra cozinha e quem era branco e bonito ia pro salão. Ninguém contratava garçom de cor”, diz. “Eu nunca falava que era cozinheiro, porque era motivo de chacota. Eu falava que sempre trabalhava em escritório.” O “Arreda Pra Cá” , produção do BHAZ , recebe o chef que, com mais de 50 anos de carreira, tornou-se um dos grandes nomes da gastronomia mineira, recebeu prêmios e reconhecimento de publicações especializadas. Em 2023, foi homenageado com o Cumbucca de Ouro por seu legado. Sua trajetória inclui trabalhos para personalidades internacionais, como o cantor Paul McCartney. 🙋🏾‍♀️ Raça e gênero “Até mesmo em candidaturas de pessoas negras, de mulheres negras , de pessoas do nosso campo, não são mulheres negras que estão pensando a estratégia, a comunicação, produzindo dados”, afirma a cientista política Myrella Santana , coordenadora da campanha de Jones Manoel (PSOL), segundo deputado federal mais votado de Pernambuco. “A campanha eleitoral precisa olhar para duas coisas simultaneamente: para as redes e para as ruas. Se você faz um trabalho excelente nas redes sociais e não consegue fazer com que a emoção, a mobilização, o sentimento cheguem nas ruas, você não está fazendo nada.” A Revista Afirmativa narra a trajetória da pesquisadora e ativista, criada na zona oeste de Recife. Filha de uma trabalhadora doméstica, ingressou na Universidade Federal de Pernambuco (UFPE) por meio da Lei de Cotas e atualmente pesquisa orçamento público, políticas públicas e participação popular. “Enquanto mulheres negras, a gente não tem muita escolha de não ligar para a política”, diz. results.evidenceText: This nonprofit has newsrooms in all 50 state capitals. Is it the future of state journalism? - Columbia Journalism Review b The Media Today Bon Secour, Ala., National Wildlife Refuge Wildlife biologist Jackie Isaacs explains the importance of habitat for foraging shorebirds. (Albert Herring/US Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Region via Wikimedia Commons) b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . In late January, after wrapping up his annual State of the State speech, North Dakota governor Doug Burgum (R) headed out to meet the press. Only two reporters awaited him: the North Dakota Monitor’s Amy Dalrymple and Michael Achterling. “Michael and I were the only ones that were there to ask him questions,” Dalrymple, a veteran reporter previously at the Bismarck Tribune , told CJR. “Because our priority is covering government, we prioritized staying there and asking the governor some questions after his speech.” The Monitor is one of the latest outlets launched by States Newsroom, a nonprofit operation whose publications on policy and politics have quickly turned it into one of the biggest players in state-level coverage. States Newsroom now has a full-time presence in all fifty states, after adding outlets in North Dakota and Utah earlier this year and establishing a partnership with Spotlight Delaware , a local nonprofit. The network now has thirty-nine freestanding newsrooms, as well as partnerships with state-focused nonprofit newsrooms in eleven states, including the Texas Tribune , CalMatters , and the Honolulu Civil Beat . Its expansion is a big part of a growing trend. According to the Pew Research Center , 20 percent of statehouse reporters worked for nonprofits in 2022, up from 6 percent in 2014. By 2022, there were almost as many statehouse reporters working for nonprofit organizations as there were working for local newspapers. States Newsroom’s team and its partners accounted for a plurality of the 353 reporters tallied in that survey. That number has grown since then: States Newsroom president Chris Fitzsimon told me that the organization now has more than 220 full-time employees, with an annual budget of more than $22 million. That rapid expansion comes as newspapers and local TV stations are retrenching , laying off reporters and cutting back on state-level coverage as they struggle to survive. ”We’re thrilled that we can fill one of the growing voids in…coverage of state government, which is the level of government that we believe has the most impact on people’s lives,” Fitzsimon said. The organization has faced criticism in the past from some media watchdogs who accuse it of harboring a left-wing bias because of its donors. That criticism was largely based on its early connection to the Hopewell Fund, a trust funded by left-leaning billionaires that incubated the organization before its launch. But States Newsroom was spun off to become its own nonprofit in 2019. It doesn’t accept any corporate donations, and publicly shares the sources of all contributions above $1,000. And while many of its larger donors lean left, it’s also received money from center-right groups like the Indiana Chamber of Commerce Foundation, as well as from nonpartisan journalism groups like the National Press Foundation and ProPublica .  While the news coverage strives to be balanced and nonpartisan, the sites’ commentary section leans left. Reporters told me that the mandate from the national office was to find people to contribute progressive-leaning commentary, though they said they were left to define what that meant to them. The only hard-and-fast rule: no commentary from current officeholders or candidates. Fitzsimon said that the newsrooms’ editorial viewpoint stemmed from his own perspective—and that donors have had no say in shaping the commentary section. “Like most legacy newspapers, we have an editorial voice and it happens to be center-left, and we have a robust nonpartisan opinion section that includes views of conservatives on a number of local issues,” he said. “Our commentary is pro-democracy, pro-transparency, and clearly labeled as opinion. Like legacy newspapers, our opinion section is completely separate from our news reporting.” But States Newsroom’s outlets are nothing like the “pink slime” organizations that pass off partisan propaganda as local news. Many of the journalists running the local newsrooms, which typically employ four to six reporters, had previously been at major state newspapers. The four States Newsroom reporters I spoke to all said they had broad leeway to run their operations as they see fit, with almost no interference from the national operation beyond a broad mandate to cover state politics and policy.  The newsrooms all have full-time reporters covering the state legislature. Some have chosen to have a full-time education reporter, while others have someone focused on agriculture, the state budget, or abortion rights. The Missouri Independent has a reporter focused mostly on cannabis (the state legalized recreational weed last year). Kathie Obradovich left the Des Moines Register to run the Iowa Capital Dispatch in early 2020 because she wanted to be “part of the solution [to] the deterioration of newspaper journalism.” She’d survived years of rolling layoffs from Gannett, her paper’s parent company, and “never really felt like I knew from day to day whether my job was secure.”  States Newsroom outlets can boast of some major scoops. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was the first to report on a lawsuit alleging that, during the early days of the COVID pandemic, a group of managers at a local Tyson pork-processing plant bet money on how many of their employees would fall ill with the deadly illness, even as they ordered them back to work. The story became international news. The Missouri Independent , partnering with MuckRock and the Associated Press, published a deeply reported exposé chronicling how federal officials spent decades downplaying the risk of radioactive waste in St. Louis—an investigation based on seventy-five years of government records, many of which had never before been publicly available. Stories like these are often picked up by other publications—which the States Newsroom outlets allow for free, so long as they’re properly credited. The States Newsroom model is promising, but nonprofit newsrooms aren’t guaranteed success. Chicago Public Media, the parent company of Chicago NPR affiliate WBEZ, was hailed as a light in the darkness when it took over the Chicago Sun-Times two years ago after years of downsizing in both newsrooms. Things are better than they were at both publications, but on Wednesday, Chicago Public Media announced that fourteen of its sixty-two unionized staff would be laid off, citing financial hardships driven by declining fundraising, listenership, and philanthropic support. Nonprofit journalism isn’t as dependent on generating revenue as traditional businesses, but it still needs to raise enough money to operate—something that depends on persuading donors to stay committed. The reporters at States Newsroom say they feel less pressure than they did at previous jobs at for-profit publications, where they had to chase clicks and worry about declining revenues. Jason Hancock, who runs the Missouri Independent , said his new job gives him “more room to breathe” than he had at his previous jobs at the Kansas City Star and St. Louis Post-Dispatch . “We can kind of step back from that and maybe, hopefully, have a little bit more perspective because we have more resources,” he said. “We’re writing our own future here.” Other notable stories: For Fast Company , Brian Stelter profiled Cesar Conde , the chair of the NBCUniversal News Group, whose leadership has been questioned since his recent hiring and firing of Ronna McDaniel, the former chair of the Republican National Committee, as a paid pundit. Though Conde spoke with Stelter prior to the McDaniel incident playing out, he had previously “hinted at the motivation” for the hire, Stelter writes, describing the news group’s philosophy as wanting “to make sure we have something for everyone.”  For Esquire , Mark Warren went deep on the story of F.L. “Bubba” Copeland , a pastor and mayor of a small town in Alabama who killed himself last year after 1819 News , a right-wing website, published photos that showed him dressed as a woman and alleged that he had written explicit fiction. “I took to asking the people in Bubba’s life what they might say to the people at 1819 News if they had the chance,” Warren writes. “Several told me that they are required to love them and will be praying for them.” Patience Haggin, of the Wall Street Journal , reports that Forbes used an alternative version of its website to run ads that buyers thought they were placing on the site itself—further proof that brands “don’t always get what they pay for” in the digital ad market. The alternative site (which Forbes shut down after the Journal inquired about it) “featured stories from Forbes.com that were stretched into formats that can fit many more ads,” Haggin writes. “One 700-word article was turned into a 34-slide slideshow.” Last year, Poland elected a new moderate government that quickly moved to clean house at the country’s state-run broadcaster , which had tilted hard to the right under the previous government. The broadcaster “now airs conventional news bulletins about domestic and international events,” the Financial Times reports —but its ratings have plunged, to the point that an upstart right-wing network, TV Republika, has overtaken it. An anchor on the latter network told the FT that it is explicitly modeled after Fox News. And GB News, an upstart right-wing network in the UK , hired Steven Edginton, formerly of the conservative Telegraph , to be its first ever correspondent based in the US—part of a broader plan to expand the network’s reach overseas. (It added an “America” vertical last year.) Geoff Marsh, the chief digital officer at GB News, told Press Gazette that “America has always been our biggest market outside the UK, both with British expatriates but also with Americans who value our British perspective on events there.” Has America ever needed a media defender more than now? Help us by joining CJR today . Cameron Joseph is a freelance political reporter with recent work in The Guardian , the Los Angeles Times , Rolling Stone , and Politico Magazine . A recipient of the 2023 National Press Foundation Dirksen Award for distinguished reporting of Congress and the 2020 National Press Club award for excellence in political journalism, he previously worked for VICE News , Talking Points Memo , the New York Daily News , The Hill and National Journal . Nagy   Reporting the Backlash The midterms pushed data centers center stage, as media, activists, and politicians questioned AI’s ever-expanding infrastructure. By Lindsay Muscato   Novaya Gazeta ’s Journalism Will Live On The paper is shutting down. But a new project grants it electronic immortality. results.evidenceText: Facing the Exits Facing the Exits “Face the Nation” boss Mary Hager is leaving CBS News, Status has learned. But she’s not the only major figure at the Sunday program saying goodbye. Oliver Darcy Nov 11, 2026 Facing the Exits “Face the Nation” boss Mary Hager is leaving CBS News, Status has learned. But she’s not the only major figure at the Sunday program saying goodbye. Oliver Darcy Nov 11, 2026 On Wednesday, "Face the Nation" boss Mary Hager had some important news to disclose to her colleagues: After more than three decades at CBS News , where she has not only led the venerable Sunday public affairs program, but also served as executive editor of politics since 2022, her time at the network was coming to an end. As Hager explained to staffers, she had made the difficult decision to leave CBS News. Hager's departure represents a significant loss for CBS News. While her official title is senior executive producer of "Face the Nation," she played an outsized role in CBS News' Washington bureau. A 35-year veteran of the network, she possesses a wealth of institutional knowledge, having helped steer its political journalism through multiple presidential elections and various political cycles. But Hager, who I’m told had informed network leadership of her intent to exit her role over the summer, isn't the only major figure at "Face the Nation" departing the show. results.pageTitle: Is It Crazy to Go to Journalism School? - Columbia Journalism Review
results.pageDescription: A student reflects on leaving the law to pursue his writing dreams.
results.evidenceText: Is It Crazy to Go to Journalism School? - Columbia Journalism Review b   The Kicker b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . Jonny Peña lived several lives before going back to school in pursuit of two master’s degrees, one in international affairs and the other in investigative journalism. Born in Colombia, he moved to Atlanta when he was four and was undocumented throughout his childhood. After earning permanent-resident status, he joined the Marines, working in Arizona, Japan, Afghanistan, and California. Then he enrolled in law school, became a prosecutor for the Manhattan district attorney’s office, took a break to work on financial crimes at a bank in Mexico City, investigated police shootings for the New York State attorney general, and went back to the district attorney’s office to work on financial fraud.  He loved working as a prosecutor. He made a salary in the mid-hundred-thousand-dollar range. But he gave it all up in hopes of becoming a journalist. He knows some people probably think he’s out of his mind, but he’s committed (even if learning to write for a general-interest audience has been tougher than he expected). I interviewed Peña about the transition, covering immigration in New York for class, and how he’s thinking about life after graduation. Listen below, or wherever you get your podcasts. results.pageTitle: The Blade’s Shocking, Inevitable News - Columbia Journalism Review
results.pageDescription: When I joined as a political writer, Toledo’s famed daily was known for its ambitious local newsroom. Now it’s preparing to publish its final issue.
results.evidenceText: The Blade’s Shocking, Inevitable News - Columbia Journalism Review b Illustration by Katie Kosma b Sign up for the daily CJR newsletter . On Labor Day, about a dozen current and former journalists from The Blade marched in Toledo, Ohio’s annual parade. Representing the Toledo NewsGuild, they carried signs drawn in marker—“Quality Work Deserves Fair Pay” and “Union Town Union Newspaper”—and wore shirts with the slogan “ The Blade Works Because We Do” spilling out of a typewriter. The next morning, Block Communications Inc. (BCI), The Blade ’s parent company, announced that the paper would close on December 31. “The financial losses The Blade has endured for years are simply not sustainable,” the company’s COO wrote in an email to the union. BCI said it was exploring a possible sale of the paper’s assets. If Toledo loses its newspaper, the city will become one of the largest in the United States without a major print or digital outlet.  The Blade ’s journalists, many of whom I worked alongside as the paper’s political writer from 2018 to 2021, had been bracing for this news since the summer, when management resumed labor negotiations with the NewsGuild. For nearly a decade, The Blade ’s unionized newsroom has been working under an expired contract; longtime guild members hadn’t seen across-the-board contractual salary increases since the early 2000s. During my time at The Blade , BCI appeared set on prolonging labor talks indefinitely as it made cost-cutting moves, such as eliminating a majority of print days beginning in early 2019. Then, this July, The Blade proposed a two-year contract that would eliminate seniority and allow guild work to be outsourced to artificial intelligence or management, terms that many members feared would hasten the newsroom’s decline. Guild members told me the company also planned to lay off a third of its seventy-five-member bargaining unit, which includes members of the ad sales and circulation teams along with journalists.  The Blade has not said whether it has fielded any interest in the paper yet. “I’m not at liberty to talk about that now,” Allan Block, the CEO of BCI, told me when I asked about the closure during a brief phone call. “Maybe in the future, but it’s still an ongoing situation, and it should be reported after the conclusion,” he added, before hanging up. Bob Cohn, the CEO of the Venetoulis Institute, which also owns the Baltimore Banner and acquired the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette from BCI in the spring, suggested in a statement that Venetoulis was unlikely to buy The Blade. “We are diligently focused on meeting the needs of readers in Maryland and Western Pennsylvania through our journalism in the Baltimore Banner and the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette ,” he said.  During negotiations, BCI told NewsGuild members that the company wanted to reach a tentative contract agreement due to what it said were mounting financial losses. (BCI did not respond to a request for comment about negotiations or layoffs.) On August 28, Toledo NewsGuild members rejected the company’s contract offer in a 45–26 vote and prepared for the worst. “We were expecting it,” Alex Bracken, a general-assignment reporter who started at the paper last year, said. “You know, you get the email from management, and it’s like, ‘Oh, wow.’ I kind of sat there for a second. Then you start digging into details and it becomes real. I mean, there’s going to be a final newspaper.” The announcement hit some of the paper’s most veteran employees the hardest. “I’m not going to say it was inevitable, but it didn’t happen overnight, or for any single reason,” Tom Henry, The Blade ’s environmental writer for the past thirty-three years, told me. It had already been a rough year for the Blade newsroom. In March, the paper’s entire staff was forced to vacate their historic headquarters because of what appeared to be maintenance problems. The ceiling was leaky and missing tiles; an editor captured a video of a bat flying around the newsroom. (BCI never shared the reason for the building’s closure.) The newsroom transitioned to working from home. Contract negotiations took place at branches of the Toledo Public Library. BCI was founded in 1900 by Paul Block, a German immigrant, initially as a media advertising firm. The company once owned publications in Ohio, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Tennessee, along with a roster of TV stations, the last of which it sold to Gray Media for eighty million dollars in May (BCI still owns Buckeye Broadband, a major cable and broadband provider in Northwest Ohio). The Blade is nearly two hundred years old, and has been in the Block family for the past century. A privately held company, BCI is headed by the Block twins: Allan, the CEO, and John, The Blade ’s editor in chief and publisher and vice-chair of the BCI board. In 2024, the brothers went to court over allegations that Allan made in a lawsuit against John and other family members, arguing they cut him out of discussions about selling the company; they resolved the suit amicably later that year. (Allan did not comment on the lawsuit. John did not respond to a request for comment.) Relations between the Blocks and their rank-and-file employees have long been contentious. “I could care less about ‘saving The Blade ,’” Susan, Allan’s wife, once commented on Facebook . “It’s way more trouble than it is worth.” In February of 2019, Pittsburgh Post-Gazette journalists witnessed John in the newsroom, allegedly intoxicated, yelling at his twelve-year-old daughter and kicking and punching a sign reading “Shame on the Blocks!” At the time, Allan said the incident resulted from the “frustration over financial and other challenges in the newspaper industry,” leading “to an unfortunate exchange with employees.” In 2022, Nolan Rosenkrans, a former Toledo NewsGuild president, recorded an encounter with Allan at an Ohio rest stop, where he confronted him about the company’s labor practices; Block cursed at Rosenkrans and appeared to swing a bag of fast food at him. The company did not respond to a request for comment about the incident, which happened the day Post-Gazette union members demonstrated outside John’s wedding. The brothers’ politics were another point of contention in the newsroom. During the 2016 presidential campaign, John and Keith Burris, The Blade ’s editorial-page editor, met Donald Trump on his private plane, which the paper mentioned in its coverage of Trump’s Toledo stop. Four years later, the paper endorsed Trump for president. (It did not endorse any candidate in 2016 or 2024.) Allan, meanwhile, has contributed to a variety of Republican campaigns, including Trump’s. In a 2022 interview with CJR , John insisted that relations with staff were never as bad as they appeared. “I get along great with the people who want to get along with me,” he said. “And in recent times, you know, some people don’t want to be my friend, which is fine.” Rosenkrans told me, “No trends in the industry or localized loss of revenue justified the way that the company has treated their staff since Allan Block took over.” He added: “It was a marked departure from how the company previously took care of staff.” Not so long ago, a job at The Blade was a dream for those starting out in the industry. In 2004, the paper won a Pulitzer Prize for investigative reporting for a series exposing Vietnam War crimes, an ambitious undertaking for a regional outlet. The following year, it broke a corruption scandal that led to the criminal conviction of Bob Taft, the governor. At the time, the newsroom employed a hundred and forty-five journalists. Over the next decade, Blade reporters took home the prestigious Livingston Award and ascended the ladder of regional and national newspapers.  Even well into the 2010s, The Blade maintained a peerless commitment to community news and a large staff, avoiding the type of mass layoffs that gutted other outlets of its size. It had an animal-welfare reporter (at the direction of John Block, who required that the paper print a “dog log” of animals euthanized at the city shelter), a dedicated obituary writer, a full-time librarian, and eight staff photographers. As The Blade ’s political writer, I reported from across the country, while my colleagues in the newsroom undertook ambitious investigations into housing, sexual abuse, and cold cases. Many of The Blade ’s journalists are now looking for new jobs. Others are planning to relocate or change careers. Bracken, who worked at a small newspaper in Peru, Indiana, that also shut down, is finding his resolve to stay in journalism diminished. “I enjoy journalism because it has an impact and makes me feel like I’m contributing something to society. But I don’t know how many more times I can jump ship for a newspaper, so it definitely has left a little bit of a sour feeling.” He added that BCI has had more than enough time to figure out how to turn a profit in the digital age. “This ultimately is a business decision that’s a consequence of the management of the company,” Bracken said, “not necessarily the individual reporters that are going to be stuck with the consequences.” Has America ever needed a media defender more than now? Help us by joining CJR today . Liz Skalka is a freelance journalist based in Maryland. She’s written for HuffPost , Politico Magazine , NOTUS , the Toledo Blade , the Los Angeles Review of Books , the New York Post , and the Stamford Advocate . View it in your browser . I watched the Online News Association’s annual conference from afar for years before I got to go to my first one. As a projects reporter at the St. Louis Beacon, it looked techy and cool and way beyond my skill set at first. But eventually, as a media reporter for Poynter, I got the chance to attend, and it blew me away.  In 2014, the conference was in Chicago, and then-New York Times staffer Amy O’Leary took the stage in a keynote about the leaked Times innovation report. I remember the whole thing feeling electric, like we were getting to peek inside change as it was unfolding.   The next year, Poynter and ONA announced a joint leadership program for women , and again, it felt like something huge was happening .  For me, the moments catching up with people in the hallways became the most meaningful experiences. But over time, there were more hallways, and a lot of conferences, where that could happen.  So when ONA CEO Niketa Patel shared a note yesterday about a “strategic shift,” it certainly felt like something big was taking place. You can read the entire note here , but the highlights (lowlights) are that the conference will pause this year and that ONA’s staff is getting cut.  I’m not sure if it’s the end of an era, the era was already over and we’re just now calling it, or this is really just a pause. I checked in with my colleague Tony Elkins (who I think I met for the first time at ONA in D.C.), about what those conferences meant to him.  “To say ONA was important to me is an understatement for two big reasons,” he told me in Slack. “First, the people I met at the annual conference have been instrumental to the rather odd path my career has taken. There have been so many hallway sessions that ultimately led me to where I am now. The second reason is that it helped me hone my skills as a speaker and a facilitator. This is foundational to the teaching I do now, and I don’t know if I would have the opportunity to speak in front of so many people, in rooms of all shapes and sizes. I really do hope the organization can find its footing because, with all credit to my favorite session by Robert Hernandez, the future of journalism feels [blank] without it.” My colleague Alex Mahadevan also found community at ONA. “ONA was particularly helpful for lonely-coder introverts like myself,” he told me in Slack. “I was pretty much the only person doing AI (internally and teaching it) at Poynter, and it was cool to meet people in the same position. To vent, of course, but also to come up with cool ideas we could use at our own organizations. I always saw NICAR as more hands-on skill-building conference, but ONA was a social one. It was super valuable to bond with a cohort." Did you go to ONA? What were your experiences? Reply to this email; I’d love to hear from you. That’s it for me. I’ve been on a tiny book tour and having the best time getting to have adventures with local journalists. 😍 Kristen Kristen Hare Faculty The Poynter Institute @kristenhare ADVERTISE // DONATE // LEARN // JOBS Did someone forward you this email? results.evidenceText: Rex Ryan Arrested For Allegedly Hitting 2 Pedestrians, Running Over Their Feet Steph Curry Demands Apology Over Wife Ayesha Criticism, Ex-NBA Stars Respond Dianna Russini: NFL And Teams Showing Sports Reporter Support Following New Gig Stefon Diggs’ Male Accuser Loses Effort to Move Case Due to NFL Star's Fans Ex-NFL Star Shawne Merriman: Late Model’s Parents Slam Move to Reduce $4 Million Win in Wrongful Death Former NFL QB Richard Todd's Wife Arrested For Domestic Violence Metropolitan Nashville Police News Rex Ryan turned himself in to authorities Wednesday morning ... after the former NFL head coach allegedly ran over the feet of two pedestrians while driving his pickup truck in Nashville. It's a shocking allegation against a guy who LOVES feet. According to Nashville PD, the 63-year-old former Jets coach was driving his truck just before midnight last Thursday when he made a right turn, running over the feet of two people who were crossing the street. Getty The alleged victims told police Ryan kept driving, but they managed to catch up to him at a red light ... where a heated argument kicked off, with Rex even getting out of his vehicle. After exchanging words, the pedestrians told cops Ryan bolted without exchanging information ... but they were able to snap a photo of his license plate. The pedestrians went to the authorities, and a warrant was issued for Rex's arrest. The charges ... two counts of leaving the scene of an accident, two counts of failing to give information/render aid, and two counts of failing to obey traffic signals. Getty His bond has been set at $6K. The whole incident is ironic, if nothing else. Back in 2010, Deadspin published videos of Ryan rubbing a woman's feet, and the jokes always been, the dude loves feet. results.pageDescription: Dianna Russini's highly anticipated comeback was over before it started as her new show couldn't even begin due to tech issues.
results.evidenceText: Dianna Russini's comeback over before it started as livestream plagued by tech issues Skip to content Credit: The Russini Report By Drew Lerner on 11/11/2026 11/11/2026 Less AI and more AA in your search results. Believe it or not, the offshore sportsbook nobody had heard of until it announced a weekly show starring Dianna Russini earlier this week wasn’t ready for its big moment. The aforementioned sportsbook, BetUS, was unable to get its livestream of The Russini Report off the ground at noon ET on Wednesday, when the show was set to make its debut. The page on its website featured an embedded video with elevator music and rotating pictures of Russini with a caption reading “show starts soon” for more than 30 minutes past 12 p.m. ET. And funnily enough, that video wasn’t even an embedded livestream, but just a 90-second clip that would play on repeat. Those who looked for The Russini Report on other platforms also struck out. The X page for the show posted a link that said “WATCH HERE” that was completely broken and didn’t even lead to a webpage. The Russini Report YouTube channel did not feature any sort of livestream. And the BetUS Vimeo account, which embedded the 90-second clip on its website, was set to private. 🚨🔴THE MOMENT IS HERE. WE ARE LIVE! 🔥 🎥WATCH HERE: https://t.co/6M35HOJrG6 🎙️🏈 THE RUSSINI REPORT with @DMRussini officially kicks off! 🔥 Breaking NFL news, insider scoops & unfiltered takes! 🏆 Bill Parcells 🎙️ @DamonAmendo 🔥 @SpikeEskin 📺 WATCH LIVE ON BETUS TV! https://t.co/pLfXt1I4x4 — The Russini Report (@RussiniReport) November 11, 2026 If there was a worst-case scenario that Russini and BetUS imagined for the show’s debut, this probably exceeded those expectations in the worst way. At 12:24 p.m. ET, nearly a half-hour after the show was scheduled to start, the show’s X handle claimed it was the overwhelming number of people trying to watch the stream that “broke it.” Well… you broke it. 😅 The premiere of The Russini Report drew a record-breaking audience today! We’re adding more seats so everyone gets in. Stay with us! We’ll be back shortly. 🙏 — The Russini Report (@RussiniReport) November 11, 2026 “The premiere of The Russini Report drew a record-breaking audience today!” the post embarrassingly went on to claim. “We’re adding more seats so everyone gets in.” How can a show that never even happened draw a “record-breaking audience,” you may ask? We’re still trying to figure that out ourselves. And for starters, blaming the people tuning in for the show for the technical difficulties, and not whoever is producing it, won’t exactly put Russini and BetUS in the good graces of the fans she’s looking to win back. It’s impossible to take this venture seriously . The X handle doesn’t even have a profile picture. This is amateur hour all around. And as this post goes live around 12:40 p.m. ET on Wednesday, there is still no show to speak of. If there’s a definition of Dead On Arrival, this could very well be it. UPDATE [12:53 p.m. ET]: The first episode of The Russini Report was posted on Vimeo about 50 minutes after it was scheduled to debut. The show appears to be prerecorded, though the original post advertising the show at noon ET seemed to suggest it’d be live. Russini also opens the show by letting viewers know she will keep an eye on emails being sent in, with the implication she’d address them live on the air. It’s unclear if the original plan was to do the show live or prerecord it. Either way, there was some mixed messaging. Russini largely stuck to football throughout the episode, though at the very end she thanks her “new family at BetUS” before thanking her “own family.” About Drew Lerner Drew Lerner is a staff writer for Awful Announcing and an aspiring cable subscriber. results.pageDescription: When pressed on the Bangladesh-made shirts, Merrin deflected by calling Kaptur pro-China and pro-Mexico, despite her votes against NAFTA and China trade relations.
results.evidenceText: Merrin's 'Made in Ohio' campaign handed out Bangladesh-made shirts — TiffinOhio.net Skip to main content Type at least 2 characters to search. local Derek Merrin is the Republican nominee for Congress in Ohio's 9th District. (Photo: Facebook) Republican congressional candidate Derek Merrin, who campaigns on returning manufacturing jobs to Ohio, distributed campaign T-shirts made in Bangladesh, Spectrum News 1 reporter Harri Leigh found. When confronted, Merrin did not address the discrepancy directly and instead accused U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur of favoring China and Mexico, despite her record opposing major trade deals with both countries. Key points Kaptur's 1993 and 2000 votes against NAFTA and permanent trade relations with China Gildan's labor-rights scrutiny over factories in El Salvador, Honduras, Haiti and Bangladesh How Kaptur's campaign sourced its shirts from a U.S. manufacturer with domestic yarns By Jen Ziegler TOLEDO, Ohio — Republican congressional candidate Derek Merrin has made bringing manufacturing jobs back to Ohio a centerpiece of his campaign against U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur. But while Merrin promises to put American workers first, his campaign has been distributing T-shirts manufactured in Bangladesh, according to an investigation by Spectrum News 1 . The October 9 report by journalist Harri Leigh documented a country-of-origin label on a campaign shirt distributed to volunteers over the summer. The shirt was manufactured by Gildan, a Canadian apparel company with factories around the world, including in Bangladesh. The findings put Merrin’s own campaign spending practices at odds with a central theme of his pitch to working-class voters in Northwest Ohio. Merrin, a former Ohio state representative seeking a rematch against Kaptur in the November 3 election, has repeatedly blamed the longtime congresswoman for the decline of American manufacturing. His campaign has distributed mailers promising good jobs, larger paychecks and products made in Ohio, according to Spectrum. But when Spectrum confronted Merrin about the foreign-made shirts and asked what standards candidates who promote American manufacturing should apply to their own campaigns, he did not directly answer. Instead, he accused Kaptur of favoring foreign businesses. “Marcy Kaptur is pro-China and pro-Mexico,” Merrin said, according to Spectrum. The accusation is particularly notable given Kaptur’s documented record of opposing major trade agreements with both countries. Kaptur opposed landmark trade agreements with China and Mexico Merrin’s suggestion that Kaptur favors China and Mexico omits two consequential votes from her congressional record. On November 17, 1993, Kaptur voted against the legislation implementing the North American Free Trade Agreement, which eliminated many trade barriers among the United States, Mexico and Canada. The legislation passed the House 234-200. On May 24, 2000, Kaptur also voted against legislation establishing permanent normal trade relations with China. That measure passed 237-197, with support from 164 Republicans and 73 Democrats. Both votes came during major national debates over whether expanded international trade would benefit American consumers and businesses at the expense of domestic manufacturing employment. Kaptur opposed the agreements despite support for them from prominent figures in her own party. Those votes do not settle every question about Kaptur’s decades-long trade record, but they provide significant context missing from Merrin’s accusation. The congresswoman opposed two of the most consequential trade measures involving the very countries he invoked when questioned about his campaign’s foreign-made merchandise. Kaptur has also publicly supported domestic purchasing requirements for federal defense contracts. Her congressional office identifies Buy America provisions as a means of helping Northern Ohio manufacturers, including tool-and-die companies, foundries and machine shops, compete for federal business. Campaign shirts linked to manufacturer with labor controversies The merchandise identified by Spectrum was made by Gildan, a major international apparel manufacturer that has faced scrutiny from labor-rights organizations over conditions in its manufacturing and supplier operations. A 2024 investigation by the Worker Rights Consortium identified Gildan among the principal buyers from APS El Salvador, a garment factory that closed in 2022 without paying workers approximately $1.9 million in wages, severance and other benefits. The organization reported recovering $1.35 million from buyers to compensate affected workers, while continuing efforts to secure the remaining funds. Spectrum also reported allegations concerning working conditions at facilities in Honduras and Haiti, as well as protests in Bangladesh following the October 2025 death of a pregnant Gildan employee who workers alleged had been denied medical leave and assistance. Those allegations concern the company’s broader operations; Spectrum did not establish that the particular factory producing Merrin’s shirts was involved in those incidents. Separately, on October 8, the Federal Trade Commission announced that Gildan and a wholesale distributor had amended a contract provision restricting discounts available to competing distributors. The agency closed its price-discrimination investigation following the change. Gildan said it had not admitted wrongdoing or paid a monetary penalty. The Spectrum investigation does not establish who selected the shirts for Merrin’s campaign, how many were distributed or where campaign graphics were printed onto them. The country-of-origin label does establish that at least some of the shirts distributed to volunteers were manufactured outside the United States. Kaptur campaign says its shirts are American-made The two campaigns have taken different approaches to their merchandise, according to the same Spectrum investigation. Kaptur’s campaign told the outlet that its T-shirts were manufactured by Royal Apparel, a U.S. company with production facilities in New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Spectrum obtained one of the campaign’s shirts and confirmed that its label identified it as made in the United States using imported yarns. Kaptur emphasized the importance of domestic production in her interview with Spectrum, saying the country needs to make products rather than merely purchase them. The distinction is especially relevant in Ohio’s 9th Congressional District, where manufacturing employment and the consequences of overseas production have been recurring political issues. Merrin has made the loss of industrial jobs a central criticism of Kaptur’s tenure, while Kaptur has spent much of her congressional career advocating for domestic manufacturing and trade protections. The candidates are facing each other for the second consecutive election. According to the Ohio Secretary of State’s official results , Kaptur defeated Merrin by just 2,382 votes in 2024, receiving 181,098 votes to Merrin’s 178,716. Libertarian Tom Pruss received another 15,381 votes. The 2026 rematch will take place under congressional district boundaries adopted in 2025. As the November 3 election approaches, Merrin has offered no direct explanation in the Spectrum interview for why a campaign built partly around bringing manufacturing back to the United States distributed apparel manufactured in Bangladesh. The original investigation did, however, establish a concrete difference in how the two campaigns sourced at least some of their merchandise. See more of our trusted coverage in your search results.
