results.pageTitle: Hundreds of ‘pink slime’ local news outlets are distributing algorithmic stories and conservative talking points - Columbia Journalism Review
results.evidenceText: Hundreds of ‘pink slime’ local news outlets are distributing algorithmic stories and conservative talking points - Columbia Journalism Review Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] " /> Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] "> Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites. In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to […] "> b Tow Report   b Editor’s Note: This is the first of our four pieces on this network. In August 2020, we found that the size of the network had nearly tripled to over 1200 sites . In October 2021, we found that the network had received funding from multiple dark money groups as well as collaborated with advocacy groups on topics to cover prior to the 2020 Election.   A n increasingly popular tactic challenges conventional wisdom on the spread of electoral disinformation: the creation of partisan outlets masquerading as local news organizations. An investigation by the Tow Center for Digital Journalism at Columbia Journalism School has discovered at least 450 websites in a network of local and business news organizations, each distributing thousands of algorithmically generated articles and a smaller number of reported stories. Of the 450 sites we discovered, at least 189 were set up as local news networks across ten states within the last twelve months by an organization called Metric Media. Titles like the East Michigan News , Hickory Sun, and Grand Canyon Times have appeared on the web ahead of the 2020 election. These networks of sites can be used in a variety of ways: as ‘stage setting’ for events, focusing attention on issues such as voter fraud and energy pricing, providing the appearance of neutrality for partisan issues, or to gather data from users that can then be used for political targeting. On October 20, the Lansing State Journal first broke the story of the network’s existence. About three dozen local news sites, owned by Metric Media , had appeared in Michigan. Further reporting by the Michigan Daily , the Guardian and the New York Times identified yet more sites. Ultimately, previous reporting has identified around 200 of these sites. Our analysis suggests that there are at least twice that number of publications across a number of related networks, of which Metric Media is just one component. Over a two-week period starting November 26, we tapped into the RSS feeds of these 189 Metric Media sites, all of which were created this year, and found over fifteen thousand unique stories had been published (over fifty thousand when aggregated across the sites), but only about a hundred titles had the bylines of human reporters. The rest cited automated services or press releases. Sign up for CJR’s daily email Many of the stories attributed to automated services (Metric Media News Service, Local Labs News Service, etc.) relied on data releases from federal programs like the Department of Education and Department of Health and Human Services, Congressional Research Service, the Federal Election Commission, and the Census Bureau. Another frequently used data sources in Metric Media’s automated stories is GasBuddy, a Boston-based startup that monitors gas station prices in North America and Australia. Some of the pieces attributed to human writers also rely on public data, from a Tax Foundation study that established the cents per gallon each state collected in wine taxes, in one instance, or a builders association study that rated structural deficiencies in bridges in another. Interspersed between stories about real estate prices and the best place to purchase premium gas based on zip code, newsier pieces appear, sometimes to quote a state senator about how the federal government should not play a role in education . Others quoted various exclusively Republican officials like US senators, chairpeople, or communications staff of the state GOP, about the impeachment process being a witch hunt or abuse of power . The networks can be traced back to conservative businessman Brian Timpone. In 2012, Timpone’s company Journatic, an outlet known for its low-cost automated story generation (which became known as ‘ pink slime journalism ’), attracted national attention and outrage for faking bylines and quotes, and for plagiarism. Journatic rebranded as Locality Labs in 2013; Locality Labs is behind many of the publications we discovered that mimic the appearance and output of traditional news organizations. These sites do not bear much information about their political use or funding, but some of them have been funded by political candidates and lobbying campaigns. Metric Media , Locality Labs (or LocalLabs), Franklin Archer , the Record Inc. , and Local Government Information Services (LGIS) are the main organizations involved in operating these networks of publications, and Timpone is associated in one way or another with each of them. Michigan Daily has detailed the convoluted relationship between these organizations. Some of these mysterious, partisan local news sites publish physical newspapers and many have minimal social media presence. At first, they do not appear to be owned by the same network or organization, but a number of clues suggest that they are intimately linked. Our analysis demonstrates the links between the networks by identifying shared markers, such as unique analytics tokens, server IP addresses, and even shared design templates and bylines on articles. Further, the Privacy Policy and Terms of Service for many of these websites—but not all—suggest they are part of Locality Labs, LLC. Websites and networks can aid campaigns to manipulate public opinion by exploiting faith in local media. The demise of local journalism in many areas creates an information vacuum, and raises the chance of success for these influence campaigns. The strategy is further made possible by the low cost of automating news stories, repurposing press releases (including obituaries from funeral homes), and replicating design templates, as well as the relative ease with which political or single-issue campaigns can obscure their funding and provenance. One in five newspapers has closed in the past decade , and many other outlets have significantly cut staff and reporting. This bleak landscape for local news creates space for this cottage industry of outlets that claim to produce journalism—typically during election cycles—and create and amplify material to support political outcomes, sometimes even physically mailing advertising materials that masquerade as newspapers but are not labeled political advertising. These publications cover certain candidates and topics, including limited government, tort reform, and labour unions, with a conservative bias. It is not clear how effective the sites are, but their architecture and strategy is useful to understand the way they co-opt the language, design and structure of news organizations. Automation has been touted as a way to create stories where there are few reporting resources, and it can be used to build credibility. It can also make a news organization look far more prolific than it is. Potentially adding to the credibility of these sites is their Google search ranking: in the case of some of the websites set up in 2015-2016, we observed that once sites had gained ample authority, they appeared on the first page of Google Search results just below the official government and social media pages. The Lansing State Journal ’s story highlights Metric Media’s intent to launch hundreds of such sites to “fill the void in local communities.” And, while Metric Media hasn’t been embroiled in controversies like its sibling organizations, the Journal’s story quotes Matt Grossmann, director of Michigan State University’s Institute for Public Policy and Social Research, who said, “many [articles] on [Metric Media site The] Lansing Sun appeared to be right-leaning.” Using multiple network analysis tools, we found at least 450 websites including the ones identified by previous reporting. There are dedicated networks with anywhere between five and forty sites per state in eleven states. Additionally, every state in the US (and Washington DC) has a dedicated “business daily” (e.g. Michigan Business Daily , Utah Business Daily ), and there are several international “business daily” websites (e.g. Toronto Business Daily, Mexico Business Daily, Manila Business Daily) as well . These are augmented by several single-subject sites (e.g. American Security News , Tobacco Newswire , Farm Insurance News ), and community sites that aggregate events, news, and business services information (e.g. Metro East Today , Wilton Review , Palmerton Guide ).   450 sites, 12 state networks, 5 corporate entities The 450 websites span twenty-one different networks operated by five distinct corporate entities. Below, we provide further detail about each of these organizations and how they’re linked. Figure 1: Breakdown of sites across networks, including the sites for multiple corporate entities or parent organizations (“Organizations”) such as LGIS, Franklin Archer, Metro Business Network, or Dan Proft’s PAC Liberty Principles. The overall distribution of sites across the networks is shown in Figure 1, with Franklin Archer’s Local News Network the single largest network with almost 130 sites. In the case of Franklin Archer, we conflated nine standalone sites that bear all the heuristics of their local news sites, even though these sites were not explicitly listed on the organization’s website. These include Surprise Journal , El Paso Review , and Lansing Reporter . With the Local News Network sites added to the 51 sites in the Metro Business network, the overall number under the Franklin Archer banner stands at 179, a close second to Metric Media, which has 189 publications across ten states. Metric Media’s North Carolina operation alone has 46 sites, making it the third biggest individual network in our dataset. For clarity, we have also conflated 25 standalone sites—sixteen topical sites, and nine international sites—under “LocalLabs: International” and “LocalLabs: Topical” in Figure 1 . These sites have a Locality Labs , LLC privacy policy or shared analytics identifier, but no other associations. In some cases, the privacy policy is not even linked on the homepage. The Mexico Business Daily , for example, doesn’t mention any affiliation in its “About Us” or “Contact” pages, and there is no privacy policy on its homepage. This link suggests it is a Locality Labs property. CISTRAN Finance follows the exact same pattern. In other cases, like the Toronto Business Daily or the Balkan News Wire , the privacy policy is linked to from the homepage, but no other affiliations are mentioned. In our analysis so far, websites on the Metric Media state-centric networks only link to other sites from the same state, including stories from Franklin Archer’s Metro Business network. There are, however, few indicators that the sites are operated by the same organization. On sites in both networks, the privacy policies and terms of service suggest they are operated by Locality Labs, LLC. Stories covering vastly different topics across the network share bylines, as well as similar—often identical—templates. These anecdotal pieces of evidence can only be gleaned after identifying the scale of the operation. To measure the scale of the operation, we relied on website metadata and network forensics: the sites shared IP addresses and various analytics identifiers. Within the same network—and even the same organization—that is expected behavior. It is highly unusual for sites to share IP addresses and analytics identifiers if they are not connected, but that’s exactly what we found in these networks, as can be seen below.   Shared IP addresses Each domain maps to an IP address, which identifies the server where the site is hosted. Across this greater network of networks, including the domains for the organizations, we found about twenty-five unique IP addresses. Some of these networks, including the biggest—Franklin Archer: Local News Network—don’t share an IP address or server with any other network as can be seen in Figure 2. Some only share IP addresses with other sites that belong to the same parent organization. For example, some state-level Metric Media properties—the publications in New Mexico, Arizona and Montana—share a server. But, Metric Media’s Maryland properties (which includes North Baltimore Journal , Harford News , Montgomery News ) also sit on the same server as the LGIS sites, which is more unusual. Similarly, it is improbable for sites within Franklin Archer’s Business Network to share an IP address with LocalLabs’ international or topical sites, unless the two organizations share resources. Some of the parent organization’s websites live on the same server as some of the LocalLabs’ topical properties, too. To wit: The Record (therecordinc.com), Franklin Archer (franklinarcher.com) and Dan Proft’s super PAC Liberty Principles (libertyprinciples.com) are on the same server as Tobacco Newswire , FDA Reporter , and FDA Health News . Figure 2: Network graph of shared IP addresses; each different edge colour represents a different IP address   Shared Google Analytics IDs Even though there were over twenty Google Analytics IDs, only five were used on more than one network. Of these, three identifiers were shared within Metric Media sites only, while another three were shared among Franklin Archer, LGIS, and the LocalLabs sites ( Figure 3 ). It is highly unlikely for independent, supposedly unrelated organizations like LGIS and Franklin Archer to share analytics identifiers. Figure 3: Network graph of shared Google Analytics IDs; each different edge colour represents a different Google Analytics ID At the time of writing, the Franklin Archer organizational website (franklinarcher.com), publications belonging to LGIS, and topical websites like American Security News , Power Newswire, and Higher Education Tribune shared the same Google Analytics ID. International sites like Gulf News Journal and a handful of business dailies also had that same identifier.   A Single Shared NewRelic ID and Quantcast ID Perhaps no other identifier illustrates the convoluted nature of these networks as well as the NewRelic ID ( Figure 4 ) and the Quantcast ID ( Figure 5 ). Most of Metric Media’s properties didn’t have a corresponding NewRelic ID, nor did the Florida network’s. ther networks, though, shared the same identifier, including Metric Media’s Maryland sites. Also, for the first time, we see the publications within the Record network, the first site of which was established in 2004, sharing an identifier with the greater network. Figure 4: Network graph of the single shared NewRelic ID Similarly, a single Quantcast identifier was used across LGIS, Record, and Metric Media sites. ( Figure 5 ). Much like the NewRelic ID, this too shows the connected nature of the networks. Figure 5: Networks connected by a single unique Quantcast ID. The Franklin Archer publications don’t seem to be relying on Quantcast identifiers at all, but Metric Media does, as do the Record network and LGIS. When we discovered the high volume of sites intricately linked across a convoluted network, we set about trying to identify the people behind these organizations, and their backgrounds. In reporting from the Lansing State Journal , Michigan Daily , and the Guardian , as well as our own analysis, one name appeared time and again: Brian Timpone. The sites in our dataset go back to 2004 with the inception of the first publication—the Madison-St. Clair Record— which is now part of the Record network. In the next section, we’ll trace through the emergence of various publications, networks, and their impact.   The Record Network The Record Network is a system of eleven publications, the first of which—the Madison-St. Clair Record —went live in 2004. The network’s publications cover the legal system in eight states; one of the outlets, Legal Newsline, is not bound to a single state. Even before Journatic was set up in 2006, Timpone was the founding publisher of sites in the Record network, which have come under scrutiny for being run by advocacy groups disguised as media organizations. Timpone is currently listed as founding publisher of the Madison-St. Clair Record and the Louisiana Record identifies him as the publisher. According to the “About Us” page on a subset of Record network sites (including Legal Newsline, Madison-St. Clair Record and Florida Record ), they are owned by the US Chamber Institute for Legal Reform , an affiliate of the US Chamber of Commerce—an organization, according to OpenSecrets , that since 2008 has been one of the biggest “dark money” spenders in US elections. Fifteen years later, these sites are still very much active.   LocalLabs/Locality Labs LocalLabs, another Timpone company, was a rebranding of Journatic in the aftermath of a 2012 scandal over plagiarism, falsified quotes , and fake bylines . For the last twenty months or so, the website for LocalLabs has simply said “We’re improving our site. Stay tuned for a new and improved LocalLabs.com.” Previously, the website detailed the services the organization provided, declaring that “LocalLabs offers community news production, advertising and advertorial content, print special sections and web and mobile application management.” We found over forty websites with the disclaimer “a product of LocalLabs” or a privacy policy/terms of service page suggesting the sites are operated by Locality Labs, LLC. Fifteen of these sites, all registered in 2018 , belong to a single network in a single state: Florida. At the time of writing, we had not found a Metric Media operation in Florida. The remaining publications are single-topic sites or international business sites. Examples of these sites include Manila Business Daily , Toronto Business Daily , and Mexico Business Daily . The single-topic sites are more US-centric, such as American Security News , American Pharmacy News, and Higher Education Tribune. While these don’t say they are a product of LocalLabs, their privacy policies are attributed to Locality Labs. Bylines on these sites are shared across other sites in other networks as well.   Newsinator and LGIS In 2015, Timpone incorporated another organization : Newsinator, a firm that, among other things, had a “history of doing paid political work and offers marketing services to companies under the name Interactive Content Services,” according to the Chicago Tribune . In 2015-16, according to the Illinois State Board of Election Expenditure data , Newsinator was paid over $300,000 for “Advertising – newspaper” by Liberty Principles , a conservative super PAC, run by Dan Proft, described as “one of the state’s most visible and controversial political figures.” According to the data, this $300,000 was split between twenty different candidates’ campaigns, most of whom were running for state office in Illinois in 2016. The line between Locality Labs and Newsinator is blurry: Proft, in his own words , works with reporters at Locality Labs and “suggests stories and discusses what rep

results.pageDescription: The race in the special election for Ohio’s open senate seat is its final stages.
results.evidenceText: Husted addresses HB6 ties, rising prices in Ohio Senate push Skip to content Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google COLUMBUS, Ohio (WOIO) - The race in the special election for Ohio’s open senate seat is its final stages. Current Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, was selected by Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine to serve the final two years of former Sen. JD Vance’s term after Vance was elected vice president. Husted is trying to stay in Washington but is being challenged by former Sen. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat, who lost two years ago to Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno. The polls have indicated this is a very close race. Some polls indicate Brown has a slight lead, others say it’s Husted. Today, I was given 15 minutes with Husted while on the campaign trail in Columbus. In our one-on-one interview, I asked about the closeness of the race and what he will try to do to win in the closing weeks. I also asked about the two areas Brown and the Democrats are using to attack Husted. First, his connection to House Bill 6 while he was lieutenant governor in Ohio, which ended up being the largest corruption scandal in state history. Husted had to testify in the trail against two former FirstEnergy executives accused of bribing lawmakers to get HB6 passed. The second area Husted is being attached to is the issues of data centers. While lieutenant governor, a number of data centers opened in the state. Husted was quick to point out that whenever a new data center would open, then-Sen. Brown was quick to celebrate the opening and send out media releases. In the above interview, Husted addresses both issues and topics on the economy and rising prices for families. results.pageDescription: As Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy came under fire for releasing an attack ad featuring his Democratic competitor Amy Acton's estranged mother, a mysterious news site was running a Facebook ad boosting the controversial video.
results.evidenceText: California conservative group linked to Ohio news site promoting Ramaswamy Acton ad - Los Angeles Times Advertisement California Mystery Ohio news site boosting Ramaswamy’s Amy Acton ad tied to conservative California nonprofit President Trump listens as gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks Oct. 12 at a campaign rally at the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, Ohio. (Jacquelyn Martin / Associated Press) By  Clara Harter Staff Writer Follow Oct. 25, 2026 8:08 AM PT 87 10 min Click here to listen to this article Share via Close extra sharing options Email Facebook X LinkedIn Threads Reddit WhatsApp Copy Link URL Copied! Print 0:00 0:00 1x This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here . See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> As Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy came under fire for releasing an attack ad featuring his Democratic competitor’s estranged mother, a mysterious news site was running a Facebook ad boosting the controversial video. The Buckeye Bulletin, which bills itself as an Ohio-based news platform committed to “reliable journalism” and “strong editorial standards,” popped up suddenly this spring and began pumping out a steady stream of pro-Ramaswamy content. The publication’s articles have no bylines. There is no list of staff. The website does not feature digital advertisements, nor does it prompt readers to subscribe, but there is also no disclosure of who is funding it. Advertisement A closer look at the Buckeye Bulletin’s Meta advertising data shows that its Facebook and Instagram accounts are managed by the Lincoln Media Foundation, a nonprofit organization affiliated with the Orange County-based Lincoln Club — the oldest and largest conservative donor organization in California. IRS documents show that the club and foundation are associated organizations and share at least two key executives. Meta’s advertising data show that the Lincoln Media Foundation manages the Instagram and Facebook accounts for the Buckeye Bulletin. (Meta) The Buckeye Bulletin, Lincoln Club and Lincoln Media Foundation did not respond to requests for comment. Advertisement The Bulletin appears to be a partisan site posing as a local news outlet ahead of the midterm elections, a strategy political scientists refer to as “pink-slime” journalism. This is not the first time a pink-slime outlet has been linked to the Lincoln Media Foundation. In 2024 Max Read, director of civic innovation for the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, identified seven such alleged outlets . With the exception of one Los Angeles-focused site, those outlets all targeted critical states for the 2024 presidential election such as Georgia, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Read reported that the media group had spent more than $63,000 on Facebook and Instagram ads, resulting in up to 18 million impressions during the last election cycle. “[The sites were] very clearly designed to try to influence the information environment ahead of the presidential election,” Read told The Times. “They had all been started early in the year and used advertising on Meta platforms to juice their engagement numbers.” When asked by The Times to take a look at the Buckeye Bulletin, Read said it appeared to be “pretty much copy and paste the same tactic that they used in 2024, even down to the aesthetics of the Facebook page and Instagram account.” “It seems like they realized this worked at some level in 2024 and is worth doing again this year,” he said. Advertisement Earlier this year, CalMatters identified another outlet tied to the Lincoln Media Foundation called the California Courier, which had been circulating Facebook advertisements criticizing Gov. Gavin Newsom and the statewide redistricting ballot measure Proposition 50. California Could this mysterious news site influence California’s 2026 election? The Courier is part of a growing ecosystem of news publications that publish biased articles in an attempt to surreptitiously influence elections. Jan. 11, 2026 Since the Buckeye Bulletin’s Facebook and Instagram pages launched in March, the outlet has shared posts touting endorsements of Ramaswamy — a biotech billionaire and former presidential candidate — as well as his platform for addressing Ohio’s healthcare crisis and his stance on religious freedom in schools. Simultaneously, the outlet’s social media posts have highlighted the refusal of his opponent — Amy Acton, Ohio’s former public health director — to debate, comments on how she “shut down” the state’s economy during the COVID-19 pandemic and a video with a watermark from right-wing political activist Laura Loomer. Last week, the outlet turned attention to Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother, Donna Arthur. In the ad, Arthur calls her daughter a liar and urges voters not to support her. However, the ad did not acknowledge that Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted for raping Acton when she was a child — an omission that drew fierce condemnation from Democrats and some Republicans, including Ohio’s Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Others, including President Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohioan, have defended the ad. Arthur and her husband fled after his 1978 indictment to Pennsylvania, where he died in 2004 without having been brought back to Ohio to face the charge. Advertisement Peppered between political content on the Bulletin’s social media feeds is a smattering of reels related to nonpolitical news, often featuring videos lifted directly from local TV stations. These other posts are used to create a “veneer of genuine local journalism,” Read said. The language on the Bulletin’s About Us page displays markers of artificial intelligence such as generic mission statements, polished but repetitive phrasing, and vague claims about journalistic standards with no details about the publication’s staff. Of the last 30 posts shared on the Bulletin’s Facebook as of 5 p.m. Friday, 21 were about state or national politics and 10 were about the gubernatorial race. Engagement on the posts dealing with Ramaswamy and Acton is consistently strong for a page with around 5,600 followers. For example, a Wednesday post on Ohio State Medical Assn.’s PAC endorsing Ramaswamy received more than 770 likes, 260 comments and 150 shares. Another video posted Wednesday with the label “Amy Acton refuses to debate, says mother is lying about her” received more than 4,800 likes, 1,500 comments and 500 shares. Meanwhile, a nonpolitical Wednesday post on a chemical explosion in Toledo received two likes, no comments and no shares. The unassuming social media scroller or person who clicked onto the website would have no clue of the Buckeye Bulletin’s apparent connection to a group of wealthy Southern California Republications. Advertisement The Lincoln Media Foundation was started by leaders of the historic Lincoln Club , which was founded in 1962 and once counted John Wayne and former President Nixon as members. Today, the club describes itself as home to “the most prominent business and thought leaders” in California and says it offers members the opportunity to meet world leaders and “experience their hobbies come to life through a combination of extravagance and leisure.” The foundation notes that it uses a digital approach to reach communities left out of the national conversation, but its website does not disclose providing funding to any news outlets. IRS records show that the nonprofit’s financial activities kicked up dramatically in 2024, the latest year for which data are available. The Lincoln Media Foundation reported $3.88 million in revenue in 2024, compared with $738,000 in 2023, $453,000 in 2022 and $415,000 in 2021. The Buckeye Bulletin’s Facebook and Instagram accounts have spent just over $10,000 boosting posts this year, according to Meta’s ad library . That’s barely a drop in the bucket in Ohio, where hotly contested races for governor and U.S. Senate have drawn hundreds of millions in spending. But presenting a slanted political view under the guise of local news tends to offer more bang for your buck than traditional advertisements, said Georgia Kernell, an associate professor in the departments of communications and political science at UCLA. Advertisement “Voters are so sick of ads; they’re getting tons of clear paid advertisements on the radio, on the television and on their social media feeds now,” she said. “Anything that can kind of look different is going to be more likely to keep their attention.” Presenting as a traditional news source also increases the likelihood of viewers believing that the information presented is well-researched, she said. Nik Usher, associate professor of communications at the University of San Diego, said it’s unclear how much influence pink-slime journalism is having on voting behavior, but political strategists are willing to try any new approach to possibly make a difference in tight races. “This is one strategic effort to throw more spaghetti at the wall, hoping it’ll stick,” Usher said. Creators of these partisan sites further stand to benefit from the fact that artificial intelligence tools are constantly scraping content from news websites without paywalls. Researchers at NewsGuard recently found that leading AI chatbots are citing pink-slime websites nearly half the time when users ask questions about candidates and issues in the midterm elections. Advertisement Democrats and Republicans have increasingly leveraged pink-slime journalism to influence voters in the past few election cycles. In 2020, the New York Times identified a network of 1,300 news sites that paid freelance writers to produce biased content for Republican groups and corporate public relations firms. In 2024, the left-leaning Star Spangled Media group used a site called the Morning Mirror to promote down-ballot Democratic candidates, according to research from Columbia Journalism School’s Tow Center for Digital Journalism. More recently, the evolution of AI has increased the ease with which these websites can be populated with content, eliminating the need to pay writers and automating the production of social media posts. Usher described pink-slime websites as “explosive bombs for public trust” that take advantage of the gap created by the loss of independent local papers and further diminish expectations for news to be fairly reported. “Once these sorts of sites are pointed out to the public it further undermines distrust in political institutions, political parties, the news media,” Usher said, “especially when AI is associated with this kind of stuff.” More to Read As local news deserts grow, nonprofit invests nearly $600 million in journalism Nov. 10, 2026 Voices Chabria: What decent people get wrong about the Amy Acton ad Oct. 25, 2026 Who is Vivek Ramaswamy and why did so many of his GOP presidential rivals attack him? results.evidenceText: A Strategic Shift for ONA - Online News Association Skip to content A Strategic Shift for ONA Date posted November 10, 2026 Posted By: Niketa Patel in Association Updates , Features , News , ONA Weekly , I have some news to share about ONA’s new strategic shift.  Since we gathered in Chicago for ONA26, many of you have asked when we will be together again. Unfortunately, it will not be in 2027. ONA has decided to pause our in-person events and will not host a conference in 2027. I want to explain why, and what happens next. First, though, I want to say what this community has meant to all of us.  Twenty-seven years of showing up In 1999, a group of journalists and technologists saw the internet as the future of journalism, years before many newsrooms were ready to agree. They built a community where the people doing this work could learn from one another and try new things together. That community became the Online News Association. In the years since, this community has been where journalism’s biggest questions about technology were asked early and most honestly. Together, we moved through the early web and into social platforms, mobile, video, data and artificial intelligence, always asking what these changes mean for the people who report the news and the communities who depend on them. Through ONA, newsrooms of every size found a common language and a place to learn. And individuals who were building non-traditional paths within journalism and felt like outsiders, the “little green martians” of their newsrooms, as former board president Charo Henríquez described us, found others trying to solve the same problems, asking the same questions and wanting to try the same experiments. For many years, the annual conference also sustained ONA’s work year-round. That is why the decision not to hold one in 2027 is one the Board and I have not made lightly. A difficult decision Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true. The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk. We worked to diversify our revenue, but the Board and I have reached the point where we must decide what ONA can continue and what it must pause.  What does this mean for the organization? This month, ONA’s long-time staff will leave the organization. Over many years, they carried this community, one conference, one program and one conversation at a time. I am grateful to them beyond what I can easily express here. I will continue to lead ONA as CEO and Executive Director, working with the Board of Directors, led by Andrew Fitzgerald, as we chart the path forward for the organization.   The Women’s Leadership Accelerator will continue on as one of ONA’s signature programs, and a call for the 2027 class will open early in the new year. Our online resources and the ONA Weekly newsletter will also continue.  What’s next? The Board and I remain committed to ONA’s mission. We are exploring partnerships and other ways to carry this work forward and to bring our community together again. We will continue to update you over time. This community has recognized excellence through the Online Journalism Awards, starting at a time when no other journalism awards program accepted online-only submissions. It opened industry doors to many, through the Student Newsroom, the MJ Bear Fellowship, the HBCU Fellowship and Women’s Leadership Accelerator. It helped people find neighbors through ONA Local and test new technologies through Journalism 360, the Challenge Fund and the AI in Journalism Initiative. The annual conference was one place we came together, but the community has always been larger than any single event. Many of you found a mentor, a collaborator, a new job or the confidence to try something new through ONA. Others took early ideas presented in the Start-Up Alley and built them into successful companies. And still others found lifelong friends and, in some cases, a spouse, by being a part of this incredible community. To everyone who has been a part of ONA as a member, speaker, volunteer, judge, sponsor, fellow, mentor or attendee, thank you. The conference was one place we gathered. But, what we have built together is bigger than any one place, and it goes with you into every newsroom and conversation you carry it to. We are so thankful for all of the love and support especially now as we embark on this strategic shift. results.evidenceText: Analysis: House Bill 6 bribery case is driving this year's Ohio AG race | WVXU, NPR Cincinnati Skip to main content Search Query Show Search © 2026 Cincinnati Public Radio Menu Show Search Search Query Donate Play Live Radio Next Up: 0:00 0:00 0:00 0:00 Available On Air Stations On Air Now Playing WVXU On Air Now Playing Radio Artifact WVXU HD2 On Air Now Playing WGUC On Air Now Playing Jazz on WGUC HD2 On Air Now Playing Inhailer Radio on WGUC HD3 All Streams Politics Politically Speaking Politically Speaking is WVXU Senior Political Analyst Howard Wilkinson's column that examines the world of politics and how it shapes the world around us. Analysis: House Bill 6 bribery case is driving this year's Ohio AG race 91.7 WVXU | By Howard Wilkinson, WVXU Published August 7, 2026 at 4:53 AM EDT Facebook Threads LinkedIn Twitter Pinterest Email Print Listen • 3:46 Facebook From left, Ohio Attorney General candidates John Kulewicz and Keith Faber. The FirstEnergy bribery scandal that came to light six years ago may soon be resolved, at long last. It was the largest bribery scandal in Ohio political history; most Ohio politicians — not to mention millions of electric rate payers — would like to see one of the most embarrassing and costly episodes in the state’s 223-year history put to rest once and for all. Two top executives ran the company that paid $61 million in bribes to push through House Bill 6, a nuclear plant bailout that cost Ohio ratepayers over a billion dollars. A grand jury indicted them , and the state has been preparing for trial. Now, with a new attorney general to be chosen by Ohio voters in November, it’s an open question whether that trial will go forward or be dismissed and go away without resolution. The two scheduled to go to trial in January are Chuck Jones, the former chairman of FirstEnergy, and Michael Dowling, a former senior vice president and chief lobbyist for the company. They are charged with allegedly bribing elected officials to pass House Bill 6. An earlier trial ended up with a hung jury on a 10-2 vote. The state came back with a new indictment , narrowing the focus of the case, after a Summit County judge threw out some of the charges. But the bribery charges remain. Regardless of whether the case goes to trial in January, the FirstEnergy scandal will be the central issue in the November election of a new Ohio Attorney General. The Democratic candidate for AG is John J. Kulewicz, a lawyer from Franklin County. He told WVXU earlier this week that if he’s elected in November, he will sign on to a January trial. He said that, of course, the two men are innocent until proven guilty, but added two separate grand juries have indicted them, including the case with a hung jury which was declared a mistrial. Kulewicz said the millions of Ohio ratepayers who were harmed by picking up the tab for what he called an illegal scheme, deserve an answer in a court of law. The Republican candidate for Ohio AG is Keith Faber, currently the state auditor and a former state representative from Celina. Faber has a much different view of this. We couldn’t reach him for comment, but he has been quoted by numerous news organizations as saying that he would want to consult with the current staff of the AG’s office before deciding whether to move forward with the case. Faber says he wants to proceed cautiously; he wants to review the files and consult with Attorney General office staff lawyers after the November election. It would be within his power to shut it down, if that’s what he decides to do. Kulewicz says Faber should recuse himself because of the substantial amount of money he has raised from energy companies. Faber, Kulewicz says, is just laying groundwork for dismissing the case. Faber and Kulewicz are about as far apart on FirstEnergy as two candidates can possibly be. Green light for Kulewicz: Proceed at the legal speed. Yellow light for Faber: Proceed with caution. The choice for Ohio voters is either push the accelerator pedal lightly or tap the brakes. Or maybe Ohio voters are ready to just blow through the red light. results.evidenceText: Toledo Blade warns it could cease to exist Skip to content Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - The city of Toledo might soon be without a daily newspaper for the first time in more than 190 years. The Toledo Blade is reporting that if Block Communications is unable to find a buyer for the newspaper, it will cease publication at the end of 2026. Leaders of The Blade say they plan to shut down by the end of the year unless a buyer steps in, putting jobs at risk and threatening the loss of a local institution. In an article published Tuesday , the paper wrote that its parent corporation was looking to sell The Blade’s assets. It went on to say that if it is unable to sell, there will be no newspaper published on Jan. 1, 2027. “Unfortunately, an extremely difficult decision has been made,” Jodi Miehls, president and chief operating officer of Block Communications, said in an email to Blade staff on Tuesday. “The Block Family’s continued investment to keep the Blade open is no longer an option. The financial losses the Blade has endured for years are simply not sustainable.” Earlier this year, Block Communications said its other major newspaper, the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette, would end publication in May. It was sold to Vernoulis Institute for Local Journalism soon after. A newspaper struggling in the U.S. in the last 20 years is not a new story, but so far The Blade has hung on, publishing material every day online. The paper is now printing two days a week. Newspaper published daily since 1835 If you only use the online version, the print edition of a newspaper may be foreign to you. But an edition of the Toledo Blade was made each day since 1835, two years before Toledo became a city. Jack Lessenberry, a former Blade writer, editor and ombudsman, said the loss of an institution like a newspaper is jarring. “I thought that for many years The Blade was the glue, the thing that bound Toledoans together. Whether they loved it or hated it,” Lessenberry said. “Not having a paper, you basically don’t have a community that has any sort of cohesion,” Lessenberry said. “Religious communities are usually held together by a sacred book. Communities, towns, cities in America, especially middle-sized cities like Toledo, were often held together by their newspaper. And the Toledo Blade was a very thorough and very responsible newspaper for many, many years.” Union responds to closure announcement Lillian King, Blade features writer and Toledo NewsGuild bargaining chair, said the jobs of the union’s 80 members are in jeopardy. She said the union negotiated for years for a fair and responsible contract. King also said the company’s proposal sought to have the union give up basic protections about job security and about the ability to trust that their work would remain their own rather than be infused with artificial intelligence, which the company refused to disclose to the public. “I’m extremely disappointed that the company has chosen to close The Blade rather than work with the Guild and work with its workers towards not just an equitable contract, but a profitable future,” King said. “You know, that’s something that we really believed in and are saddened to experience this outcome.” The full statement from the Toledo NewsGuild, including additional details on the contract vote and comments from King and Toledo NewsGuild President Mac Arnold, is below. Full statement from the Toledo NewsGuild The Toledo News Guild released the following statement Tuesday following The Blade’s announcement: The Toledo Blade ended employees’ Labor Day weekend with an email Tuesday morning announcing it would close on Dec. 31 if it is not sold by then. Prior to the announcement, the company had asked union employees to vote for a contract proposal that would have cut their severance in half, in addition to greenlighting giving away their work to AI, among other outsourcing. Workers voted that down, 46-25. Union members’ objections were largely non-economical. This was reflected in Guild counterproposals. Following the vote, Blade Guild members returned to the bargaining table offering yet another compromise to the Company on Thursday. The Block Communications Inc. board met the next day. “It’s disappointing that Block Communications would rather shutter the paper than work toward an equitable contract. The Company’s proposal would have axed seniority, halved severance for its most experienced employees, and allowed the outsourcing of all Guild work. All content at The Blade could be created or edited with AI, with no protections for journalists or requirements to disclose AI usage to its readers,” said Lillian King, Blade features writer and Toledo NewsGuild bargaining chair. “Signing that contract would have meant signing away our self-respect, and with it, Toledo’s mandate for ethical journalism. After nearly 200 years of operating one of the nation’s great newspapers, Toledo deserves better,” King said. In its attempts to pressure workers into voting to cut their severance in half, Blade management also made clear that doing so would not necessarily keep the paper open, either. “Blade workers would welcome new ownership that shares our commitment to local news as well as to the people of Toledo, and would look forward to working with any such prospective buyers,” said Mac Arnold, Blade outdoors writer and Toledo NewsGuild president. results.evidenceText: Gary Click lashes out after weakest win of his Statehouse career — TiffinOhio.net Skip to main content Type at least 2 characters to search. local State Rep. Gary Click, a Republican from Vickery, represents Ohio's 88th House District. (Screenshot via The Rooster / Facebook) State Rep. Gary Click, R-Vickery, won reelection Tuesday with 58.57% of the vote over Tiffin City Councilman Aaron Jones, his weakest showing since 2020, after Ohio House Republicans supplied $92,765.80 in advertising and printing. Click then called Seneca County Democrats disgraceful and TiffinOhio.net a fake news blog. Key points How Click compared with other Republicans on the same ballot in both counties Click's unsupported claim that dark money from Chicago was used against him Why Jones's concession call went unanswered and how Jones described his campaign's goals By R.L. Porter State Rep. Gary Click (R-Vickery) won reelection Tuesday with the weakest performance of his Statehouse career after receiving nearly $93,000 in advertising and printing support from the Ohio House Republican establishment. By Wednesday, he was lashing out at Democrats and the press, declaring an exception to his “usual practice” of being gracious in victory. Click defeated Democrat Aaron Jones, a Tiffin city councilman, by 23,930 votes to 16,927, according to unofficial returns from the Seneca County and Sandusky County boards of elections. Click received 58.57% to Jones’s 41.43%, an eight-point decline from his 2024 vote share and more than nine points below his 2022 performance. Campaign-finance records reviewed by TiffinOhio.net show that the Ohio House Republican Organizational Committee, known as OHROC, reported $92,765.80 in in-kind contributions to Click’s campaign in its 2026 pre-general filings. Seven transactions included $91,124.33 in advertising and $1,641.47 in printing. Click’s own pre-general report separately listed more than $18,000 in cash expenditures by his campaign committee. That substantial financial backing accompanied Click’s weakest general-election result since he first won the House seat in 2020. He received 62.90% that year, 67.80% in 2022 and 66.57% in 2024. His 2026 performance was also the weakest Republican showing in any contested District 88 midterm election since the district began encompassing Seneca and Sandusky counties in 2012. Republican Bill Reineke received 59.01% in 2014 and 65.87% in 2018. Jones’s 41.43% was the strongest Democratic share in a District 88 midterm during that period. Click also ran behind other Republicans on Tuesday’s ballot. Across the same two counties, state auditor candidate Frank LaRose received 62.27% of the two-party vote, Attorney General Keith Faber received 62.02%, and state treasurer candidate Jay Edwards received 61.44%. Click lashes out as Jones congratulates him Following the election, Click used his campaign’s Facebook account to acknowledge that he ordinarily believes winners should be gracious before launching into attacks against his political opponents. “It has been my custom to be gracious in victory. I think that is normally the right thing to do,” Click wrote. He singled out Seneca County Democratic Party leader Gina Grandillo and the county’s Democrats, calling their conduct “disgraceful and disgusting.” He also attacked this outlet, TiffinOhio.net, which he described as a “fake news blog.” On his personal Facebook account, Click separately accused opponents of spreading personal smears and alleged that “dark money from Chicago” had been used against him. His posts provided no documentation identifying the alleged funding or substantiating the accusations. Jones took a different approach. In his public concession statement Tuesday night, he congratulated Click, thanked campaign volunteers and expressed hope that the incumbent would listen to residents concerned about property taxes, public schools and working families. A source within the Jones campaign told TiffinOhio.net that Jones personally called Click at approximately 9:30 p.m. Tuesday to congratulate him and concede the race. Click did not answer, and Jones left a voicemail. According to the source, Click had not returned the call as of Wednesday. Nearly $93,000 in GOP support after a primary scare The substantial OHROC investment followed a Republican primary in which Click nearly lost his nomination to Eric Watson, a first-time candidate from Tiffin. Watson defeated Click in Seneca County and finished just 600 votes behind him districtwide, receiving 47.72% of the Republican primary vote. Watson mounted that challenge despite substantially weaker fundraising and a series of extraordinary claims about data centers. In February, The Toledo Blade reported on a recording supplied by Click in which Watson claimed artificial intelligence data centers could harvest people’s conscious and unconscious thoughts, including while they slept. Click’s campaign had already benefited from OHROC support during the primary. Campaign-finance filings reviewed by TiffinOhio.net showed Click’s committee transferred $45,000 to the Republican caucus organization, which subsequently reported providing $38,611.62 in campaign support. Click reported $69,461.37 in contributions through primary day, nearly four times Watson’s $17,488.05. The incumbent ultimately survived both elections with the backing of Republican leaders and the party’s campaign apparatus. Jones, who said his campaign was outspent by a wide margin, nevertheless secured the strongest Democratic midterm performance in the district in more than a decade. Click’s renewed attacks on Seneca County Democrats also followed his own documented false allegations against local political opponents. In August, campaign-finance records disproved his assertion that Jones, Grandillo and Fremont City Councilwoman Angie Ruiz had contributed to Watson’s Republican primary campaign. None had done so. Click deleted the accusation and acknowledged his mistake. Three months later, Click celebrated his reelection by accusing opponents of dishonesty and alleging political funding from Chicago. His victory posts offered no evidence supporting those accusations, even as his own campaign-finance disclosures documented tens of thousands of dollars in advertising supplied by the Republican establishment. View it in your browser . OPINION Face the changes: Two top leaders are leaving CBS News’ ‘Face the Nation’ Margaret Brennan on the set of CBS News’ “Face the Nation” in 2020. (Courtesy of CBS News) There’s a big shakeup at CBS News as Mary Hager, senior executive producer of “Face the Nation,” prepares to leave the network after 35 years. Status’ Oliver Darcy broke the news, writing , “Hager’s departure represents a significant loss for CBS News. While her official title is senior executive producer of ‘Face the Nation,’ she played an outsized role in CBS News’ Washington bureau. A 35-year veteran of the network, she possesses a wealth of institutional knowledge, having helped steer its political journalism through multiple presidential elections and various political cycles.” Hager was first named executive producer of “Face the Nation” in 2011, and became CBS News’ executive editor of politics in 2022. As Darcy noted, Hager is senior executive producer of “Face the Nation.” It turns out that Anne Hsu, the program’s executive producer, is also leaving. Darcy writes that Hsu is moving to the network’s bureau in Hong Kong. Darcy writes, “The loss of both Hager and Hsu will leave the program without two of its most senior editorial leaders at a particularly precarious moment for CBS News, which has been navigating an incredibly turbulent year under new Editor-In-Chief Bari Weiss, particularly with the upheaval at ‘60 Minutes.’ The exits of Hager and Hsu will present Weiss with an opportunity to effectively reset ‘Face the Nation’ and steer the influential program more to her liking. While the Sunday show has not been a primary focus of Weiss’ since she took the reins at CBS News, she has privately mulled its future.” Several reports indicate that Hager’s retirement had been planned and was not a sudden decision. She reportedly called the decision difficult. Nevertheless, Hager’s retirement and Hsu’s departure are likely rattling those at the program. The Guardian’s Jeremy Barr tweeted that CBS News president Tom Cibrowski met with the “Face the Nation” staff on Wednesday to not only celebrate Hager’s legacy on the show, but to “ease concerns.” Hager does leave the show in good shape. Variety’s Brian Steinberg wrote , “She will leave ‘Nation’ as the show is faring well in the ratings. Season to date as of November 8, ‘Face The Nation’ has won more viewers than either NBC’s ‘Meet The Press’ or ABC’s ‘This Week.’ And while it has lost some viewership compared to last season, the show has seen a surge among viewers between 26 and 54, the demographic coveted most by advertisers — and leads its rivals in that category as well.” One more thing to keep in mind: Darcy reported Wednesday that earlier this year, Weiss quietly explored the idea of replacing Margaret Brennan as moderator of “Face the Nation,” but, Darcy wrote, “that potential move never seemed to materialize.” Darcy added, “Now, with two of the show’s most influential editorial figures on their way out, Weiss will have an opportunity to — at the very least — install her preferred leadership and move the program in a different direction.” Biden looks back Former President Joe Biden has been in the news a lot lately. That’s because he has a memoir coming out next week: “Promise Me, America” On Wednesday, People magazine published a Q&A he did with Nick Maslow: “Joe Biden, in His Only New Interview, Goes on Camera with PEOPLE to Talk About Everything.” Well, not quite everything. But they did hit on plenty of topics: Biden’s prostate cancer, his marriage and family, his faith, and of course, his thoughts on the presidency and Donald Trump’s redecorating of the White House. Maslow asked, “What’s your reaction to the Trump ballroom and the East Wing being destroyed?” Biden said, “Almost as disturbing as the gold bars on the walls of the White House and the Oval Office. I mean, what the hell are we talking about? I find it disturbing. … I’ve viewed the president’s judgment in tearing down the East Wing and a number of other things as nothing more than to try to create monuments to himself: ‘I built that.’ I find it beneath the country.” Biden was also asked if he would have done anything differently in 2024. Biden said, “What I can’t say, because there’s no evidence of it — if I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would’ve not gone forward, because I don’t think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for (president). But that wasn’t the case. … I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job.” Caught on video U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, and his wife Jennifer Rauchet attend a ceremony at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va. on Wednesday. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) One day after House Republicans blocked an effort to impeach him, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his entourage were verbally reprimanded by a soldier guarding the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier after someone in the group laughed loudly. Following a Veterans Day ceremony, Hegseth went to the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery with his wife, Jennifer Hegseth, chief of staff Ricky Buria, deputy chief of staff Patrick Weaver and senior adviser Tami Radabaugh. As the group dispersed after posing for photos near the steps, someone laughed. A U.S. Army sentinel guarding the tomb turned toward the group and yelled, “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!” CNN ran a video of the incident. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement, “The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored — and will always honor — the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe. While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum.” Bad news at ONA The Online News Association has canceled its annual conference for 2027 and is parting ways with its longtime staff. ONA executive director and CEO Niketa Patel said in a note that it was a difficult decision, writing, “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true. The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk. We worked to diversify our revenue, but the Board and I have reached the point where we must decide what ONA can continue and what it must pause.” My Poynter colleague Kristen Hare wrote in her Local Edition newsletter , “I’m not sure if it’s the end of an era, the era was already over and we’re just now calling it, or this is really just a pause.” Tony Elkins, a faculty member at Poynter, told Hare, “To say ONA was important to me is an understatement for two big reasons. First, the people I met at the annual conference have been instrumental to the rather odd path my career has taken. There have been so many hallway sessions that ultimately led me to where I am now. The second reason is that it helped me hone my skills as a speaker and a facilitator. This is foundational to the teaching I do now, and I don’t know if I would have the opportunity to speak in front of so many people, in rooms of all shapes and sizes. I really do hope the organization can find its footing because, with all credit to my favorite session by Robert Hernandez, the future of journalism feels (blank) without it.” Poynter faculty member Alex Mahadevan, the director of MediaWise, told Hare, “ONA was particularly helpful for lonely-coder introverts like myself. I was pretty much the only person doing AI (internally and teaching it) at Poynter, and it was cool to meet people in the same position. To vent, of course, but also to come up with cool ideas we could use at our own organizations. I always saw NICAR as a more hands-on skill-building conference, but ONA was a social one. It was super valuable to bond with a cohort.” Watch your feet What is it with Rex Ryan and feet? Ryan, the former NFL coach who is now an analyst on ESPN, turned himself in to Nashville police on Wednesday after allegedly running over the feet of two pedestrians while driving his truck downtown last Thursday night and then fleeing the scene. He faces six misdemeanor charges — two counts each of ​​leaving the scene of an accident, failure to provide information or render aid and disobeying a traffic signal. Awful Announcing’s Matt Yoder wrote , “Of course, anyone in the know will find that to be incredibly ironic given Ryan’s well-documented love of that particular body part.” Reports are that the pedestrians had the right of way in a crosswalk as they attempted to cross Broadway in the heart of Nashville’s bar and music district. After allegedly hitting the pedestrians while making a turn, Ryan kept on driving. The pedestrians were able to catch up with Ryan when he stopped at a nearby traffic light. Ryan reportedly got out of the truck and argued with them before getting back in and driving off again. Photos were taken of his license plate and reported to police. The pedestrians allegedly suffered minor injuries. In a statement, ESPN said, “We are aware and are in touch with Rex.” Ryan, 63, is the former head coach of the New York Jets and Buffalo Bills, and joined ESPN in 2017. He is a regular on shows such as “Sunday NFL Countdown” and “Get Up,” as well as “SportsCenter.” TMZ first reported the news of Ryan’s arrest. Did they work?” The Wall Street Journal’s Noah Higgins-Dunn and Amrith Ramkumar with “Three States Where the AI Boom Could Slow After the Midterms.” For The Atlantic, Kyle Berlin with “The Worst Thing About AI Writing.” Awful Announcing’s Drew Lerner with “Dianna Russini’s comeback over before it started as livestream plagued by tech issues.” Hot type The Atlantic’s Ali Breland with “The Christian Nationalists Have a Plan.” More resources for journalists Strengthen your leadership skills with Poynter Leadership Academy , designed for experienced newsroom leaders with at least three years of management experience. While the era didn’t end well, the current incarnation of the New York Jets has a lot of fans wistful for the days of Rex Ryan. The former Jets head coach took the franchise to back-to-back AFC Championship games and they haven’t even been back to the playoffs in the 13 seasons since. While Aaron Rodgers has helped keep the Jets in the New York tabloid headlines all season long, Ryan had a few controversies of his own while in town. None more memorable than the 2010 revelation that he and his wife had made a foot fetish video that appeared on the internet. While he and the Jets initially tried to deflect attention from the viral video, he would eventually become more playful about it and his interest in feet. These days, it’s not uncommon to see one of his ESPN colleagues or other NFL folks make a foot joke at Rex’s expense while he laughs along with them . Ryan appeared on The Pivot this week where the topic of his foot fetish was broached. The ESPN NFL analyst adamantly defended his appreciation of his wife’s toes. My Birkin, type shit pic.twitter.com/Tfqax1kRoz — Chairman of #FeetFridays and #SolesSaturday (@FlyoutChase) October 23, 2024 “I love my wife’s feet,” said Ryan. “I don’t know what it is. But if a chick’s got jacked-up feet, I’m out. I don’t care how gorgeous. I’m out. I don’t know what the hell it is. Some people are boob guys, leg guys. Of course, I notice a pretty gorgeous face, whatever… but I’m checking the feet out.” Ryan added that he thought his wife was “gonna frickin’ kill me” when the video went viral but was shocked to find out that many of his Jets players admitted they had a similar fetish. “Now I have fun with it and it’s like, yeah, that’s me. That’s who I am.
